title: Selling the dream
body:
Learning to sell

Jordan Belfort discovered early that he liked selling things. As a teenager, he sold Italian ices and earned enough money to take his ambitions seriously. He wanted a comfortable life, but comfort alone would never have satisfied him. He wanted the sort of wealth other people stopped to look at.

He briefly considered dentistry. The prospect of years of training for an ordinary professional income did not appeal to him, so he left. A business selling meat and seafood seemed more promising. He could knock on a door, start a conversation and persuade someone to buy something they had not planned to buy that morning.

Orders came in, but delivering them was harder. Food spoiled, bills went unpaid and customers did not always receive what they expected. The business failed. Belfort had found that he could sell. He had also found that enthusiasm on a doorstep could not keep a badly organised company running.

His next opportunity was in finance. At the brokerage firm L. F. Rothschild, he learned how brokers talked to clients and how they presented investments. He watched the confidence of people who seemed completely at home around large sums of money. Then the stock market crashed in October 1987, and he lost his job.

Afterward, Belfort began selling penny stocks. These were cheap shares in small companies, often difficult to sell again and far riskier than his customers understood. What interested him most was the commission. A broker could keep a large part of the money from a sale. For someone good on the telephone, that made each successful call unusually rewarding.

The customer did not need to understand the company in detail for Belfort to make a sale. He could describe an exciting future, suggest that other investors would soon discover the opportunity and make waiting sound like a mistake. Questions about the business became interruptions to a conversation about getting rich.

Inside Stratton Oakmont

With a partner, Belfort built Stratton Oakmont. The name suggested an established institution. The business grew from an ordinary office filled with people making telephone calls. Many recruits had little experience of financial markets. Some had worked in bars or left college. Their most useful qualification was a willingness to keep selling after a stranger said no.

Belfort taught them how to control a conversation. A hesitant answer from a potential customer was a problem to overcome. The broker would return to the possible profit, introduce more urgency and steer the discussion toward a purchase. The method could be taught and repeated, which allowed the firm to grow beyond Belfort's own calls.

People answering those calls often had modest savings and little experience of investing. They heard someone who sounded informed and certain. A retirement fund, money saved for children or the proceeds of a loan could become the basis of a purchase. The broker's confidence made a risky decision feel considered.

The firm also manipulated share prices. It obtained shares cheaply, then used its sales force to encourage customers to buy them. As demand increased, the price rose. That rise helped the sales pitch because brokers could point to a stock that appeared to be doing well. Those controlling the shares could then sell their holdings at the higher price.

Customers who bought near the top were left with the losses when the price fell. The money had already moved. A company did not need to become more productive or sell a better product for the people running this scheme to profit. They needed other people to keep buying until they had sold their own shares.

Within the office, successful brokers received bonuses, expensive gifts and attention. Those who performed badly could be humiliated or dismissed. The pressure to sell affected what employees were willing to ask. Doubts about a company were inconvenient when a manager wanted another completed order.

Belfort's own spending became part of the attraction. He bought expensive cars, houses and a yacht. Employees could see the rewards he promised. The parties and widespread drug use made the office increasingly difficult to separate from the life he lived outside it. People were encouraged to admire the excess while overlooking where the money came from.

Complaints and records

As Stratton Oakmont expanded, investors began complaining. Some had watched shares lose most of their value after being urged to buy them. Regulators examined suspicious activity. Employees who questioned what they were selling faced pressure to carry on.

Hiding the proceeds created further problems. Money moved through companies and accounts overseas. Accounts held under other names made ownership harder to follow. Belfort treated these arrangements as protection, but investigators were interested in the route the money had taken and why it needed to be concealed.

His private life was also deteriorating. Drug use damaged his relationships and his judgment. Arguments at home accompanied the pressure building around the business. His wealth allowed him to keep spending, but it did not make the consequences disappear.

The loss of his yacht in 1996 became one of the best known episodes of that period. Belfort insisted on a voyage in dangerous weather despite warnings from the captain. The boat took on water and the people aboard had to be rescued. It was an expensive disaster that could have ended much worse.

For investigators, bank records mattered more than the spectacle. FBI agent Gregory Coleman worked through evidence of Belfort's financial dealings. Transactions could be compared with reported income, property purchases and the accounts given by people who knew the firm. A telephone promise might vanish as soon as a call ended. The movement of money left a record.

Former employees helped the investigation. Some faced legal trouble of their own. Others had reasons to stop protecting their employer. Recordings and documents made it harder for Belfort to control the story. People who had once depended on the business were now describing how it worked.

The investigation eventually reached Belfort himself. He faced serious fraud and money laundering charges. Rather than continue defending everyone around him, he cooperated with the authorities. Information about colleagues and associates became part of his effort to reduce the consequences he faced. Employees who had learned the business from him also faced prosecution.

Another way to make money

Belfort served twenty two months in prison. During that time, he began turning his experiences into a story. Fellow prisoner Tommy Chong encouraged him to write about what had happened. There was plenty of material: the sales calls, the money, the drugs and the effort to keep everything from collapsing.

His memoir, The Wolf of Wall Street, appeared in 2007. Readers encountered the events through the voice of the man at their centre. The excesses that had surrounded the fraud became scenes people wanted to read. A second book followed, and the story eventually reached Hollywood.

In 2013, Martin Scorsese's film starring Leonardo DiCaprio brought Belfort's name to a much larger audience. Viewers watched lavish parties and reckless behaviour, often presented with humour. The film made the world of Stratton Oakmont vivid, but the attention also helped turn Belfort into a celebrity.

For the investors, the aftermath was much less entertaining. Losing savings can mean delaying retirement, taking on debt or abandoning plans that took years to finance. A film deal for the person responsible does not replace that money. Nor does it return the time people spent trying to recover their losses.

Belfort was ordered to pay about 110 million dollars in restitution. The order required him to repay the people harmed by the fraud. The size of that obligation helps explain why his later public career attracts criticism. Money earned from telling the story exists alongside money owed to the people harmed by it.

He went on to work as a speaker and sales trainer. The ability to hold an audience, which had helped him sell shares, could also help him sell advice. His reputation made people curious enough to listen, even when that reputation came from a conviction for fraud.

There is a practical question for anyone listening to a persuasive salesperson: what can be checked independently? A confident voice does not explain a company's finances. An exciting account of future profits does not make those profits certain. At Stratton Oakmont, customers made decisions without receiving an honest account of the risks or of the broker's interests.

The firm's growth depended on those decisions being repeated, call after call. Its collapse ended the operation, but the losses remained with the people who had trusted it. Belfort gained another audience through books, film and public appearances. His former customers were still dealing with what happened after they put down the telephone.

title: When the boom ended
body:
Buying a better life

In the United States of the 1920s, a new car or radio could make the future feel close enough to touch. Factories produced goods that had once seemed expensive or unusual. Electricity changed homes and workplaces. Cars created demand for steel, rubber and oil, while roads and petrol stations connected more of the country.

Mass production helped manufacturers make goods more quickly. More people could buy them, especially if they did not have to pay the full price immediately. Instalment plans divided a purchase into smaller payments. A household could take a radio home and pay for it over the following months, provided its income continued.

The prosperity was uneven. Many farmers had expanded during the First World War, when demand for food was high. Afterward, falling agricultural prices made debts harder to repay. Buying machinery could increase output without solving the problem of low prices. A farmer might produce more and still struggle to meet the next payment.

In growing cities, those difficulties were easy to overlook. New buildings, busy shops and popular entertainment offered visible signs of success. Credit allowed spending to run ahead of the money people already had. As long as wages and sales continued, the next payment could seem like a manageable concern for another day.

The same confidence reached the stock market. Rising share prices attracted people who hoped to increase their savings quickly. Some bought shares with borrowed money. They paid part of the purchase price themselves and borrowed the rest, using the shares as security. This was known as buying on margin.

Borrowing increased the possible return on the investor's own money, but it also increased the danger. A fall in the share price reduced the value securing the loan. A lender could demand more money or require the shares to be sold. Someone who had expected to profit from rising prices could instead be forced to sell into a falling market.

During the boom, that possibility received less attention than stories of easy gains. Stock tips passed between friends and strangers. A price that had risen yesterday seemed like evidence that it would rise again tomorrow. Warnings that prices had become detached from the strength of the businesses behind them were unwelcome.

The crash and what followed

In October 1929, selling overwhelmed the market. Black Tuesday, October 29, became one of the best known days of the crash. Investors tried to dispose of shares as prices fell. People who had borrowed to buy them faced demands they could not always meet. Wealth recorded on paper disappeared as buyers withdrew or offered much lower prices.

The crash was a major shock, but the Great Depression was not a single bad day on the stock exchange. Economic activity had already begun to weaken. Over the following years, falling production, banking crises and unemployment reinforced one another. Families who owned no shares could still lose their jobs or their savings.

Banks depended on borrowers repaying loans. When businesses failed and households lost income, more loans went unpaid. Depositors then worried about whether their bank could return their money. If enough people tried to withdraw savings at once, the bank could come under severe pressure.

The banking panics did not all happen immediately after the crash. Waves of failures and withdrawals followed during the early 1930s. A closed bank could leave families unable to access the money they needed for ordinary expenses. It could also leave a local business without the credit it used to pay workers or buy supplies.

An employer losing customers cut production. Reduced production meant fewer hours or fewer jobs. Workers with less income bought less from other businesses. Each decision could seem necessary to the person making it while adding to the problems faced by someone else.

The crisis spread beyond the United States. International loans and trade connected economies that had not fully recovered from the First World War. When American finance became harder to obtain, countries that depended on it faced new pressure. Falling demand and declining trade made recovery more difficult across national borders.

Trying to get through the week

By 1933, roughly a quarter of the American civilian labour force was unemployed, according to historical estimates. Behind that figure were households trying to work out which expenses they could postpone. Rent still had to be paid. Children still needed food and clothes. Finding another job became harder when many neighbours were searching too.

Breadlines and soup kitchens became familiar sights. People who had previously supported themselves needed help to eat. A factory worker could return to the gates repeatedly without knowing whether work would resume. Families delayed plans that once seemed ordinary, including marriage, a home or children.

In parts of the Great Plains, the economic crisis was accompanied by an environmental disaster. Drought struck land made vulnerable by farming practices. Strong winds carried away dry soil. Dust storms damaged crops and filled homes, turning the ground on which families depended into a source of danger.

People left farms and travelled in search of work. California became a destination for many, but reaching another state did not guarantee a job or a decent place to live. Migration exchanged a familiar hardship for an uncertain situation. Families carried what they could and tried to earn enough to stay together.

President Herbert Hoover encouraged voluntary assistance and introduced measures intended to support recovery, but he resisted the scale of direct federal relief many people wanted. Settlements of makeshift shelters became known as Hoovervilles. His name was attached to the visible evidence that families could no longer afford proper housing.

In 1932, veterans of the First World War travelled to Washington to demand early payment of a bonus that was not yet due. They needed money during the crisis and established camps while pressing their demand. The removal of the protesters by the army, including the use of tear gas and the destruction of camps, deepened anger at the government.

Work, relief and new rules

Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in March 1933, amid a severe banking crisis. His administration moved to stabilise the banks and restore confidence. The New Deal brought a range of programmes addressing immediate hardship and the institutions that shaped economic life. They developed over several years rather than arriving as a single finished plan.

The Civilian Conservation Corps employed young men on conservation work, including planting trees. Public employment programmes later hired people to build and repair roads, schools and other facilities. Receiving a wage allowed workers to buy necessities while producing things their communities could use.

The Tennessee Valley Authority developed projects that included dams and electricity generation. Such investment changed the opportunities available in a region where many households had lacked electricity. Recovery meant different things in different places: a wage, a safer bank account or a service that had previously been out of reach.

Financial reforms aimed to reduce the danger of another collapse. Deposit insurance gave savers protection within the scheme's limits. The Securities and Exchange Commission became responsible for overseeing securities markets and enforcing rules. Social Security established a system intended to provide support in old age and other forms of protection.

Artists and writers also found work through federal programmes. Photographs and accounts from the period recorded families on the road, people seeking work and the conditions in which they lived. These records preserved details that national figures could not show, including the effort required to get through an ordinary day.

Recovery was incomplete and uneven. New Deal measures helped many people and changed the role of government, but they did not bring the Depression to a clear end during the 1930s. Another recession in 1937 interrupted the improvement. A family that had recently regained an income could once again face insecurity.

The approach of the Second World War changed demand for American production. Orders and government spending expanded, and factories produced equipment and supplies for war. The return to full employment was bound up with that mobilisation. It was not simply the final step in a smooth recovery from the stock market crash.

The Depression lasted long enough to shape decisions far beyond the years of the crisis. For people who had lost a job, a farm or access to their savings, promises of permanent prosperity could sound different afterward. A radio bought on credit had once represented an affordable future. During the Depression, the next payment could become a problem a family had no way to solve.

title: Beyond the bookstore
body:
A business on the road

In 1994, Jeff Bezos left a well paid job in New York and travelled west with his wife, MacKenzie. He was preparing to sell books over the internet. During the journey toward Seattle, he worked on the business plan from the passenger seat. The company he was imagining would need customers who were willing to order from a screen and wait for a parcel.

Bezos had studied electrical engineering and computer science at Princeton. His early career took him through technology and finance, eventually to the investment firm D. E. Shaw. He had a promising position there when the rapid growth of internet use caught his attention. Leaving meant giving up a career that was already going well for an idea whose customers barely existed yet.

Books offered a practical starting point. There were far more titles than an ordinary shop could keep on its shelves. A website could present a much larger selection. Books were also standardised products: a customer searching for a particular title could identify it without first holding it or trying it on.

The name Amazon suggested the scale Bezos hoped to reach. The early operation was much smaller. Desks made from doors became part of the company's story about saving money. Staff had to build the website, handle orders and work out how to get books to buyers. A good idea still depended on a parcel reaching the right address.

Amazon was founded in 1994, and its online store opened in July 1995. Orders arrived from beyond the local area. For customers, the appeal included being able to find a title that a nearby bookshop did not stock. They could search from home rather than call several shops or travel between them.

More than a catalogue

The website gradually became a place to compare products as well as buy them. Customer reviews allowed people to describe what they liked and disliked. A negative review might discourage an immediate sale, but useful information gave a customer a reason to return. Shopping involved reading other people's experiences, not just the description provided by a seller.

Amazon went public in 1997 while it was still building the business. Bezos argued for investment in future growth rather than an emphasis on immediate profit. That approach required shareholders to accept substantial spending and uncertainty. Growing sales alone did not settle the question of whether the company could become financially durable.

The product range expanded beyond books into music, films, toys and electronics. Every new category brought more possibilities for customers and more complications for the company. Products had to be stored, described, located and delivered. A larger catalogue was useful only if the systems behind it could handle the extra work.

In 2000, Amazon Marketplace opened another route to expansion. Other merchants could sell through Amazon's website. This meant the selection could grow without Amazon buying and owning every product itself. A seller gained access to shoppers, while Amazon became the place where those shoppers searched, compared and placed orders.

The arrangement also changed Amazon's relationship with businesses using the site. They were customers of its services and competitors in retail. A merchant could depend on the platform for sales while competing with products Amazon sold directly. The convenience of gathering buyers and sellers in one place came with questions about who controlled that place.

Surviving the crash

The collapse of the internet investment boom in 2000 exposed weaknesses across the technology sector. Investors who had been excited by fast growth started asking more urgent questions about costs and profits. Amazon's share price fell sharply. Its future no longer seemed assured simply because more people were shopping online.

Inside the company, cost cutting meant layoffs and reduced spending. Projects were reconsidered, and operations had to become more efficient. Employees felt the difference between a business trying to expand quickly and one under pressure to show that it could survive. Many other internet companies did not make it through this period.

Amazon continued operating, but survival required more than keeping the website online. A retailer needs to know what it has, where it is and when it can deliver it. Warehouses, transport arrangements and software became central to the company's development. Improving these systems could reduce mistakes and make delivery promises more credible.

Fulfilment centres brought large quantities of goods into organised networks. Scanners and software helped track items through storage, packing and shipment. For a customer, the process might look like a few clicks followed by a knock at the door. Behind it were workers, equipment and decisions about where stock should be held.

Speed became something customers could expect rather than an occasional extra. That expectation placed demands on the organisation providing it. A promise made on a product page had to be supported by the people and facilities responsible for the order. The simplicity of the purchase depended on considerable work out of sight.

A subscription, a reader and a cloud

Amazon introduced Prime in 2005. Customers paid a membership fee for benefits that included fast delivery on eligible purchases. Once someone had paid, ordering again could feel easier than comparing the delivery charges at another shop. The subscription encouraged repeated use of the same retailer.

For customers, Prime offered a predictable arrangement. For Amazon, it created a reason to maintain the relationship beyond a single sale. It also made delivery capacity important to the value of the membership. A subscription promising convenience would lose its appeal if orders regularly failed to arrive as expected.

The Kindle, introduced in 2007, returned the company to books in a different form. A reader could buy a digital book and read it on a device instead of waiting for a printed copy. Publishers and booksellers now had to consider a market in which the store, the delivery process and the reading device could all be linked.

Digital books did not eliminate printed books. They added another way to distribute and read them. Amazon's position in that market gave it influence over how readers discovered titles and how publishers reached those readers. The change involved commercial relationships as well as the replacement of paper with a screen for some purchases.

Another important expansion was less visible to shoppers. Amazon Web Services began offering infrastructure services in 2006. Businesses could obtain computing resources and storage through a service rather than buy and manage all the necessary equipment themselves. What a customer needed could change as a project grew.

This became a business serving organisations whose customers might never visit Amazon's shop. A company could use computing services while selling an entirely different product. Amazon had developed an additional source of income from infrastructure, alongside the infrastructure that moved physical goods.

The businesses reinforced the company's broad presence, but they were not identical. Selling a book, delivering groceries and providing computing capacity involved different customers and operational problems. Describing everything as online shopping missed how far Amazon had expanded beyond its original catalogue.

The costs of convenience

Expansion also brought criticism. Merchants questioned the power Amazon held over access to customers. Concerns included how products appeared in search results and whether information obtained through operating the marketplace could give Amazon an advantage as a competing retailer. Amazon disputed accusations that its practices were improper.

These disputes were about more than whether customers liked low prices. A merchant could build a successful business through a platform and still have little control over the conditions of access. Changes to visibility or service terms could affect sales. The platform's responsibility toward businesses depending on it became a matter of public debate.

Workers raised concerns about conditions inside fulfilment centres, including demanding targets and monitoring. A fast delivery promise did not reveal what a shift felt like for the people picking and packing products. Reports about working conditions brought attention to labour behind a service presented to shoppers as almost effortless.

Traditional retailers also faced growing competition. They had to invest in online sales and delivery while continuing to run physical shops. Amazon contributed to that pressure, but the failure of any individual chain could have several causes. Treating every closure as the result of one competitor would hide differences in debt, management and customer demand.

Amazon's purchase of Whole Foods in 2017 added a large physical grocery business. It showed that stores and online operations could be combined in the same organisation. The company also expanded its presence in entertainment and home devices. Its services reached people during activities well beyond placing an order for a book.

Some businesses associated with Bezos remained separate from Amazon. His purchase of The Washington Post was personal, through a private company. Blue Origin was his separate space venture. Keeping that distinction matters when considering what Amazon owns and what belongs to its founder's other activities.

A different role for the founder

In 2020, Bezos appeared before Congress as lawmakers examined the power of large technology companies. The hearing brought questions about marketplace practices and competition into public view. The company had become large enough that its decisions affected many businesses outside its own workforce.

In February 2021, Amazon announced that Andy Jassy would become chief executive later that year. Jassy had led Amazon Web Services. Bezos moved into the role of executive chair in July. He stepped away from running daily operations, but he did not disappear from the company or give up every formal responsibility.

The change gave him more time for other interests, including Blue Origin. His enthusiasm for space had been part of his life long before Amazon. By then, however, the retailer was an organisation with its own employees, systems and customers. Its operation could no longer be understood only as the decisions of one founder.

The distance between the first online book orders and that leadership transition was considerable. Amazon had learned to manage physical deliveries, attract independent sellers and provide digital services to other organisations. Customers encountered different parts of it without necessarily seeing how those parts connected.

A parcel arriving quickly can be useful. A business renting computing resources can avoid buying equipment before it needs it. Those benefits coexist with questions about competition, working conditions and dependence on powerful intermediaries. Understanding Amazon means looking at both the service visible on a screen and the arrangements that make it possible.

title: Building Claude
body:
A new research company

In May 2021, a small artificial intelligence company announced that it had raised 124 million dollars. Anthropic wanted to build systems that people could understand and direct more reliably. Dario Amodei led the company as chief executive, while his sister Daniela served as president. Members of the team had already worked on some of the research behind large language models.

They entered a field where progress was difficult to predict. A model trained on large amounts of text could produce fluent answers to questions it had never encountered in exactly that form. It could also invent an explanation and present it with the same confidence as a correct answer. Better writing did not necessarily mean better judgment.

For a person trying a chatbot for fun, an absurd answer might be amusing. In a workplace, the same mistake could cause trouble. Someone might copy an incorrect statement into a report or trust a piece of code without noticing a flaw. As models became more useful, there were more reasons to take their limitations seriously.

Anthropic's founders had left OpenAI to establish their own company. They wanted to make safety and reliability central to their research. That ambition still required a working product. A system that avoided every difficult question would be of little use to customers, while a system that answered everything could create other problems.

The team faced a practical question: how could it teach a model to respond helpfully while setting meaningful limits? Writing a rule was easier than making the system apply it consistently. The same word could refer to something dangerous in one conversation and something ordinary in another. Understanding the request mattered as much as recognising its vocabulary.

Learning from principles

One established training method used human feedback. People compared answers and indicated which they preferred. Those judgments helped guide further training. The process could improve behaviour, but collecting detailed feedback took time and effort. It also raised questions about whose preferences the system was learning.

Anthropic explored an approach called Constitutional AI. A written set of principles guided a model as it criticised and revised responses. Further training used comparisons informed by AI feedback. People still chose the principles and designed the process. The approach reduced the need for certain human labels rather than removing human decisions from the system.

The name could make the method sound more settled than it was. A constitution did not guarantee that every answer would be correct or every refusal sensible. Researchers still had to test the model and examine failures. A useful assistant needed to recognise legitimate requests as well as harmful ones.

Meanwhile, the cost of the work continued to grow. Training larger models required computing infrastructure and people able to build and study them. In April 2022, Anthropic announced a funding round of 580 million dollars. Money gave the team room to expand its experiments, but it did not settle whether those experiments would become a sustainable business.

Late in 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. The public could suddenly try a conversational AI system without needing to understand the research behind it. Anthropic was developing its own assistant, Claude, in a market where many potential users had already formed expectations around a competitor.

Finding useful work

Anthropic introduced Claude more broadly in March 2023, after testing with partners. It could help with writing, questions and tasks involving text. A customer could use a chat interface, while developers could connect the model to other software through an API. The company needed to show where those capabilities could fit into daily work.

Long documents offered one opportunity. In May 2023, Anthropic expanded Claude's context window to 100,000 tokens. A token is a unit used by the model to process text, and does not always correspond to a whole word. The company estimated that this window could hold roughly 75,000 words.

That capacity allowed users to provide much more material in a single interaction. A business could submit a long report or a collection of documents and ask questions about them. A programmer could include more of a project when asking for help. There was less need to cut everything into small, disconnected pieces.

A context window was not permanent memory, however. It described how much material the model could work with in an interaction. Nor did accepting a long document prove that every detail would be understood correctly. The result still needed checking, especially when a small mistake could change a decision.

For businesses, the attraction was concrete. Reading and comparing documents took time. A system that could help locate relevant passages or explain a difficult section might be useful even if it could not replace a person's judgment. Customers could evaluate it against tasks they already had, rather than against a distant promise about artificial intelligence.

The money behind the models

Amazon and Google became important partners and investors. Their involvement brought access to resources that a young research company could not easily build alone. Large models needed computing capacity, and cloud providers had both the equipment and relationships with business customers. The partnerships connected research to infrastructure and distribution.

Those arrangements also reflected competition among technology companies. Microsoft had a close relationship with OpenAI. Amazon and Google had reasons to support other developers and make their models available through their own services. Investing in a model company offered a stake in its progress, while supplying computing resources supported the work required to make that progress possible.

Anthropic introduced the Claude 3 family in March 2024. Haiku, Sonnet and Opus offered different balances of speed, cost and capability. A customer did not necessarily need the largest model for every request. A simpler task might be handled more cheaply, while a demanding one could justify additional resources.

The models could also process images, including charts and diagrams. This made them relevant to documents whose meaning depended on more than written paragraphs. Anthropic published favourable benchmark results, but a test score could not establish performance on every customer's work. Choosing a model still involved trying it on the actual task.

The company now had more than one way to reach customers. Some wanted a conversational assistant. Others wanted a model inside an existing product or business process. Their expectations differed, and so did the consequences of failure. A useful demonstration had to become a service people could depend on repeatedly.

From answers to actions

Software development offered another opening. A chatbot could already suggest code, but a developer often had to copy the suggestion, find the right file and test it. If something failed, the developer returned with another question. Much of the practical work remained between one answer and the next.

Claude Code brought the model into that workflow. Anthropic released it as a research preview in February 2025. The tool ran in a terminal and could examine files, edit code and run commands. It could use the results of a test to guide another attempt, rather than stopping after producing a proposed solution.

This changed the kind of task a developer could assign. Instead of asking for a short example, someone could ask the tool to investigate a bug across a project. The system might need to read several files before suggesting a change. Running tests gave it information about whether the change worked, although passing tests could not prove everything was correct.

The value depended on the work involved. A tool that handled a routine change well could save time. A mistaken edit could also create more work for the person reviewing it. Giving a model access to commands and files made its behaviour more consequential than an incorrect paragraph in a chat window.

Developers therefore had to consider what the tool could access and which actions needed review. The promise was practical assistance with software work. It was not evidence that every engineering task could be delegated successfully or that responsibility for the resulting program had disappeared.

Limits and investors

The question of acceptable use became especially visible in Anthropic's dealings with the United States military. In February 2026, the company described a disagreement over two restrictions: mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. Anthropic said it supported other lawful national security uses but would retain those limits.

In March, it said it had received notice designating it a supply chain risk. Anthropic disputed the action and said it would challenge it in court. It also argued that the restriction concerned use connected directly to defence contracts, rather than every activity of every business with military customers. Those were the company's stated positions in an ongoing dispute.

The disagreement made the commercial consequences of a safety policy visible. Restricting a customer's use could put a contract at risk. Accepting every requested use could conflict with the reasons the company had given for setting limits. The pressure existed alongside the continuing expense of research and infrastructure.

On June 1, 2026, Anthropic announced that it had confidentially submitted a draft registration statement for a proposed public offering. The announcement did not set a share price or the number of shares. It said the offering would depend on market conditions and other factors. Filing documents gave the company an option to proceed, rather than a guaranteed outcome.

Private investors had already helped finance the development of Claude. A public offering could bring another source of capital, along with shareholders judging the company's spending and prospects. Claims about a final valuation remained separate from what had actually been announced. At that point, the price of an eventual offering was still undecided.

title: Rockets that return
body:
Before the launch pad

On June 12, 2026, SpaceX began trading on Nasdaq. Its shares had been priced at 135 dollars, and the initial offering raised 75 billion dollars before any additional shares from the underwriters' option. The company arriving on the stock market included a launch business, satellite communications and, following an acquisition, artificial intelligence. Its history had begun with a much smaller rocket.

Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002 after making money in internet businesses. He had grown up in South Africa, moved to Canada and then continued his education in the United States. Computing interested him early. Before trying to send hardware into space, he had worked on getting information and payments to move through computer networks.

In the 1990s, Musk and his brother Kimbal helped build Zip2, which supplied online business information and city guides to newspapers. The idea connected familiar local information with a new way of reaching readers. A newspaper could offer more than a printed page, while businesses could appear in a directory people accessed from a computer.

Growing a company also meant dealing with investors and changes in management. Musk did not retain full control over the business he had helped establish. Compaq acquired Zip2 in 1999, giving him money to invest elsewhere. His next major venture, X.com, focused on financial services over the internet.

X.com merged with Confinity, and the combined business became PayPal. Musk lost his position as chief executive but remained a shareholder. In 2002, eBay acquired PayPal in a transaction valued at about 1.5 billion dollars. The sale gave him resources for ventures whose risks were quite different from those of an online payment service.

Building a rocket company

SpaceX needed engineers, equipment and somewhere to test the things it built. A software error might be corrected and deployed again. A failed launch could destroy the vehicle and its payload in seconds. Each attempt depended on the interaction of engines, structures and control systems, with little room for error once the rocket left the ground.

The first vehicle was Falcon 1. The team operated from Omelek Island in the Marshall Islands, far from the offices and factories associated with the American technology industry. Moving equipment and preparing launches in that setting added practical difficulties to the engineering work. A launch was the visible end of a long chain of tasks.

Falcon 1's first flight, in March 2006, failed. The second attempt also failed to reach orbit. A third flight in August 2008 ended after a problem during the separation of the rocket's stages. Each failure produced information, but collecting information this way was expensive. The company still had to build another vehicle and get it ready.

By 2008, Musk was also deeply involved in Tesla, the electric car company. Both businesses needed money while trying to solve difficult production problems. The financial crisis made the search for funding harder. Investors had reasons to be cautious, and a promise of future success did not pay the bills arriving that month.

The fourth Falcon 1 launch took place on September 28, 2008. This time the rocket reached orbit. It became the first privately developed rocket using liquid fuel to do so. For SpaceX, that result demonstrated something its earlier attempts had not: the vehicle could complete the central task the company had built it to perform.

Success did not erase the cost of the failed flights. It did give the company a stronger basis for seeking work. In December 2008, NASA awarded SpaceX a contract worth 1.6 billion dollars for twelve cargo supply missions to the International Space Station. The contract linked the company's future to deliveries that other people would depend on.

Delivering and coming back

SpaceX developed the larger Falcon 9 rocket and the Dragon spacecraft. Its work expanded from proving that a vehicle could reach orbit to providing a transport service. A customer paying for a mission needed more than an impressive demonstration. The cargo had to arrive, and the provider had to prepare for the next flight as well.

In May 2012, Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to attach to the International Space Station, deliver cargo and return to Earth. The mission was part of a broader change in how NASA obtained transport services. SpaceX now had experience operating around a destination occupied by people, with requirements extending well beyond the launch itself.

Another problem concerned what happened to expensive hardware after it had done its first job. A conventional rocket discarded stages as it climbed. Much of the vehicle was lost after a single flight. SpaceX wanted to recover the first stage of Falcon 9 and eventually use recovered boosters again.

Getting a booster back was difficult. It had to separate, change its path and control its descent. Landing required accurate timing and enough remaining propellant. Several attempts ended in crashes or explosions. A video of a failed landing showed only the final seconds of work that included calculations, manufacturing and repeated adjustments.

In December 2015, a Falcon 9 first stage returned to a landing pad in Florida and stood upright. Above it, the second stage continued the mission to put communications satellites into orbit. The returning booster had not travelled all the way around Earth. It was one part of an orbital launch vehicle coming back after completing its part of the ascent.

Recovery opened a path toward using costly components on later missions. The financial benefit depended on how much inspection and repair a booster needed, as well as how often it could fly. A landing alone did not establish a new price for every launch. Reuse had to become a repeatable process that customers could trust.

Satellites and a larger vehicle

Starlink gave SpaceX a continuing reason to launch large numbers of satellites. The network supplied internet connections through satellites in orbit, including to places where conventional connections were limited. It connected the launch business with a communications service used by customers on the ground.

Launching satellites for its own network differed from carrying a single payload for an outside customer. SpaceX had to consider the network as a whole, with spacecraft working together to provide service. Launch capacity was one part of that operation. The equipment used by subscribers and the communications links also had to work.

The company also pursued Starship, a much larger vehicle intended to carry people and cargo on ambitious missions. Musk's plans included travel to Mars. Such plans created demanding engineering goals, but a proposed destination was not an accomplished journey. Development still required tests, infrastructure and regulatory permission.

The distinction mattered when discussing the company. Falcon missions, satellite internet and future travel to Mars were related through SpaceX, but they were at different stages of development. A customer using an internet connection was buying an existing service. An investor considering a distant space mission was evaluating a prospect with unresolved difficulties.

Meanwhile, Musk became involved in more businesses. He bought Twitter in 2022, later renamed it X, and founded xAI in 2023. His interests now included a social platform and the development of artificial intelligence models, alongside electric vehicles and space transport. These activities involved different customers, costs and competitors.

A company with several businesses

In February 2026, SpaceX announced that it had acquired xAI. The transaction brought artificial intelligence into the space company's organisation. It also brought together activities that investors would have to examine jointly, rather than treating SpaceX solely as a provider of rocket launches.

One proposed connection involved computing in orbit. Artificial intelligence required large amounts of computing capacity, and operating that capacity required energy and cooling. Musk's vision connected launch vehicles, satellite communications and computing infrastructure in space. It was a proposal about what those businesses might eventually make possible together.

The proposal still required technical and economic answers. Launching equipment was only one part of operating a computing service. Investors had to consider whether the combined businesses could deliver the promised benefits and what it would cost to build the necessary systems. Ownership of several technologies did not itself settle whether a particular project would work.

The public offering brought those questions to a wider group of investors. SpaceX announced the offering price on June 11, 2026, with trading beginning the following day. Nasdaq reported an initial offering valuation of approximately 1.77 trillion dollars. That valuation described the company through the price of its shares, rather than money sitting in a bank account.

Musk's personal wealth was a separate question. Estimates of an owner's wealth depend in part on the assessed value of their holdings, and those values can change. A company's market value is not identical to its founder's wealth, nor does an increase in share price mean the founder has received that amount in cash.

At the time of the offering, SpaceX had travelled from repeated failures of Falcon 1 to operating launch and satellite businesses. It had also taken on new activities through acquisition. Public investors were buying into that mixture of operating services and future plans. The capital raised could support further work, while the company still had to manufacture hardware, serve customers and complete the next mission.

title: Making other people's chips
body:
A factory without its own product

In 1987, Morris Chang helped establish a semiconductor company with an unusual promise. It would manufacture chips for other businesses without selling its own competing brand of chips. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, usually called TSMC, offered customers a place to turn their designs into physical products. A designer could concentrate on what a chip should do while another company handled its production.

Chang had spent much of his career in the American semiconductor industry. Born in China in 1931, he moved to the United States as a young man and studied engineering. His work included many years at Texas Instruments. By the time he arrived in Taiwan in 1985, he understood the difficulties of manufacturing chips as well as the commercial decisions surrounding that work.

Taiwan's government wanted to develop a strong semiconductor industry. The Industrial Technology Research Institute provided part of the foundation for that effort. Chang's proposal gave it a particular direction: build a business around manufacturing for customers rather than trying to sell another line of finished chips. Government support and investment from Philips helped make TSMC possible.

Many important semiconductor companies combined design and manufacturing. They decided how their chips would work and operated the factories that made them. This arrangement gave them control, but it also required enormous investment. A promising design did not pay for a fabrication plant, and a new company could struggle to afford both.

There was also a question of trust. A designer giving sensitive plans to another manufacturer wanted to know how those plans would be treated. If the manufacturer sold a competing product, the relationship could be uncomfortable. TSMC's commitment to manufacturing services gave customers a reason to consider handing over their designs.

Customers arrive slowly

The early years did not immediately prove that the idea would transform the industry. Chang later described the first customers as established manufacturers providing work that was not always stable. Small companies also placed orders, initially in Taiwan and later in the United States. Filling a factory required a steady flow of work, not simply interest in a new business model.

Growth became stronger as more companies chose to design chips without owning fabrication plants. These businesses became known as fabless companies. They still needed someone to manufacture their products, but they could devote more of their own resources to design and sales. The foundry model gave them a way to enter markets without building every part of the production chain themselves.

TSMC's opportunity expanded with that change. A customer might have an idea for a communications chip or a graphics processor and need a factory capable of making it reliably. The two companies had different responsibilities, but the final product depended on their cooperation. A design had to work with the manufacturing process chosen for it.

This division did not make manufacturing a simple service anyone could copy. Producing chips involved many precise steps. A factory had to control its processes closely and keep improving the proportion of products that worked correctly. Customers cared about the number of usable chips they received, as well as the capabilities promised on paper.

That proportion is often called yield. A process that could make a remarkable chip occasionally might still be too expensive for a mass market product. Reliable output mattered because failed chips consumed materials, equipment time and money. Learning how to reduce defects was part of the expertise a foundry sold.

Building for the next generation

The business also required investment before demand was certain. Equipment and new facilities could take years to prepare. Waiting until every order was confirmed could leave a manufacturer without enough capacity when customers needed it. Building too much could leave expensive equipment underused when sales slowed.

Technology downturns made those choices harder. The collapse of the internet boom and the financial crisis of 2008 affected demand across the industry. Customers adjusted plans, and manufacturers had to decide what spending they could sustain. Research and capacity investments might support future work even while current orders weakened.

TSMC's development was therefore more complicated than a sequence of smaller numbers on a technology chart. It involved funding, production experience and relationships with customers. A new process had to become useful at commercial scale. The company needed to deliver what it had promised while preparing for products customers had not yet released.

Smartphones increased the importance of that preparation. A successful device could require huge quantities of chips within a demanding schedule. Apple became a major TSMC customer, while other designers also needed advanced manufacturing. A large order offered revenue, but fulfilling it required capacity and consistent results across many units.

The relationship mattered to both sides. Designers wanted chips suited to their products, and the manufacturer needed information that helped it plan. Neither side could treat the other as an interchangeable detail. Changing a design or moving production could involve substantial work rather than a quick switch between suppliers.

What the small numbers mean

Semiconductor manufacturing generations are often described using numbers measured in nanometres. These names help distinguish processes, but they should not be read as a direct measurement of an entire chip or every feature inside it. Comparing manufacturers requires more than choosing the smallest number in an announcement.

Performance, energy use and the amount of circuitry that fits into a given area all matter. So do cost and suitability for the job. A processor used for demanding computation has different needs from a component controlling a simple function. Not every useful chip requires the newest manufacturing generation.

This is one reason it is misleading to describe TSMC as the maker of all the world's chips. Semiconductor production includes many kinds of products and many manufacturers. Memory, logic and specialised components serve different purposes. TSMC is especially important in contract manufacturing, but that market is not identical to the entire semiconductor industry.

Market share figures also depend on what is being counted. A percentage for foundry revenue cannot automatically be treated as the share of all chips produced. TSMC itself has used a broader definition called Foundry 2.0 that includes additional manufacturing services and activities. Numbers based on different definitions can describe different markets even when they appear side by side.

In its report on 2025, TSMC said its technology known as two nanometres had entered volume production in the final quarter of the year. This was a manufacturing milestone, rather than a claim that every customer had already moved to that process. Older generations continued to have uses, and demand came from several kinds of devices.

When chips were missing

During the pandemic, shortages made the dependence on semiconductors visible outside the technology industry. Car production could be interrupted because a necessary component was unavailable. A vehicle contained electronics for many different functions, and missing one required part could prevent completion of the whole product.

Demand changed quickly. People bought equipment for working and studying at home, while manufacturers in other sectors revised their orders. When demand returned or shifted again, chip production could not instantly follow. Factories already had customers waiting, and increasing capacity took time.

The problem was broader than one company choosing between cars and games consoles. Production capacity, materials and later stages such as assembly and testing could all become constraints. A supply chain had to deliver the right component, not simply a large number of some other chip.

In January 2022, the United States Department of Commerce published findings from a supply chain inquiry. For the difficult semiconductor products identified by responding buyers, median inventories had fallen from forty days in 2019 to fewer than five days in 2021. With so little stock, even a brief interruption could stop production elsewhere.

Governments and companies began paying closer attention to where essential components were made. A low purchase price was only one consideration. Dependence on distant suppliers could leave a factory exposed to events it could not control. Building more capacity looked attractive, but it could not solve an immediate shortage overnight.

More factories, more dependencies

Taiwan's importance in advanced semiconductor manufacturing also raised concerns about conflict and disruption. A concentration of important factories meant that trouble in one region could affect customers far away. Some observers described this importance as a possible deterrent to conflict. It was not a guarantee that political or military risks would disappear.

Nor would taking control of a building automatically give someone a functioning chip industry. Manufacturing depended on trained people, equipment, materials and continuing relationships with suppliers. These connections crossed borders. The value of a factory rested partly in work and knowledge that could not be reduced to the ownership of its walls.

Expanding production abroad was one response to concerns about concentration. TSMC developed manufacturing operations in Arizona. In March 2025, it announced plans to add 100 billion dollars to its earlier 65 billion dollar investment programme in the United States. The planned expansion included more fabrication plants, advanced packaging facilities and research activity.

Announced investment was not the same as completed capacity. A new site needed workers, suppliers and processes that functioned together. Experience from existing operations could help, but construction alone did not reproduce every part of an established industrial network. Customers needed reliable output from the new facilities, not merely new buildings.

TSMC's customers might put their own names on the devices people bought, leaving the manufacturer's role less visible. Yet the separation between design and production remained central to the business. Each new product still required a design that could be manufactured, a process that worked consistently and enough capacity to deliver the chips when they were needed.

title: Money without a bank
body:
A proposal during a crisis

In 2008, the financial crisis damaged confidence in banks and the institutions responsible for supervising them. Lehman Brothers collapsed, governments arranged emergency support, and many households faced losing their homes. Against that background, a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a proposal for a different kind of electronic payment system.

The Bitcoin paper appeared in October 2008. It described how people could send payments without relying on a financial institution to maintain the central record. The problem was familiar in digital systems: if information can be copied, how do you prevent someone from spending the same money twice? Bitcoin proposed a shared transaction history supported by cryptography and computing work.

The first block was created in January 2009. It included a newspaper headline about another possible bank rescue. The message connected Bitcoin's beginning with the financial events around it, although it could not explain every intention of its unidentified creator. At first, the network was a small experiment followed by people interested in computers and digital money.

In 2010, a transaction involving ten thousand bitcoins and two pizzas became an enduring part of Bitcoin's history. It showed that someone was willing to exchange the new currency for an ordinary purchase. Later price increases made the quantity seem extraordinary. At the time, participants were still discovering what people might actually do with the system.

A record shared across a network

Bitcoin groups transactions into blocks linked to earlier blocks. Participants running validating software check whether proposed transactions and blocks follow the rules. They do not need to accept a changed record merely because someone announces that it is correct. The network's checks are essential to the way it operates.

Miners compete to produce a valid proof of work. This requires repeated calculations and consumes electricity. A successful miner can propose the next block, receiving a subsidy and transaction fees when the block becomes part of the accepted chain. Other participants still check its validity. Computing power does not make an invalid payment valid.

The system makes rewriting established history costly, rather than literally impossible. An attacker with sufficient mining power could attempt to reorganise recent transactions or spend the same funds twice. That does not mean the attacker can freely take coins from any address. Describing the ledger as unhackable hides the conditions under which its protections operate.

The network also differs from the services people use to access it. An exchange may hold assets for customers, while someone managing their own wallet controls the necessary keys. Theft, lost credentials or a dishonest service can cause losses even when the underlying transaction rules continue working.

Scarcity and price

Bitcoin's issuance follows a schedule in its existing rules. The subsidy began at fifty bitcoins per block and is reduced by half after each interval of 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years. The schedule approaches a limit of twenty one million bitcoins. This differs from a currency whose monetary supply is managed by a central bank.

A limited supply does not establish a stable price. People can become more or less willing to buy Bitcoin, and the amount they will pay can change sharply. Scarcity is one reason supporters value it, but scarcity alone cannot guarantee purchasing power or future returns. Holding it can involve substantial losses as well as gains.

Supporters often compare Bitcoin with gold. They point to its limited supply and the possibility of transferring value without transporting a physical object. Critics note that Bitcoin does not itself produce rent, profits or dividends. The disagreement concerns what gives an asset value and how much buyers should be willing to pay.

These arguments cannot be settled simply by pointing to a past price increase. A person who bought at one moment may have had a very different experience from someone who bought later. Expectations about future demand influence the price, and expectations can change. A technology can continue operating while its market price falls.

Experiments beyond the computer screen

Bitcoin attracted people interested in international payments and alternatives to existing financial services. Sending value across borders was an appealing possibility. The practical result depended on access, fees and the way recipients converted or spent what they received. It was not automatically instant or free in every situation.

El Salvador adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 and supported a public wallet. The experiment drew attention because a government was promoting use beyond a small group of enthusiasts. Announcing a policy, however, was different from achieving widespread everyday adoption. People still needed reasons to use the system for purchases and payments.

In 2025, reforms made private sector acceptance voluntary and required taxes to be paid in United States dollars. The International Monetary Fund described these changes as part of efforts to address risks associated with the project. The history therefore included policy revisions, rather than a simple progression from adoption to universal use.

Who can change the rules?

Satoshi eventually stopped participating publicly. Bitcoin continued without an identifiable founder directing every decision. Its software could be examined and proposals for changes discussed. A proposal still needed adoption by participants. Authorship of the original system did not give someone a special password for changing everyone's rules.

Agreement could be difficult because users had different interests. Developers, miners and businesses might disagree about a change. That process was not a single worldwide vote in which every person had to approve every update. The software people chose to run helped determine which rules they accepted.

Governments could also affect mining businesses, exchanges and access to financial services. A distributed network was not a promise of immunity from regulation or practical disruption. Bitcoin's operation, its legal treatment and its market value remained separate questions. A payment still depended on valid authorisation, acceptance by the network and someone willing to receive it.

title: Buying Hollywood
body:
In October 2026, the companies behind Batman, Harry Potter, CNN and CBS came under the same corporate roof. Paramount completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, and the combined company took the name Skydance. A business that had recently been much smaller than its target had managed to buy it. The explanation lies in the difference between what a company is worth on the stock market and how much money it can persuade other people to provide.

The deal carried an announced enterprise value of about 110 billion dollars. That number included debt as well as the value paid for shares. It did not mean that Paramount had kept 110 billion dollars in a bank account, waiting for the right studio to appear. The purchase depended on investors, lenders and the expectation that the enlarged business would earn enough money to support its obligations.

A different route into film

David Ellison entered Hollywood with advantages few aspiring actors could imagine. His father, Larry Ellison, had helped establish Oracle and accumulated an enormous fortune. In 2006, David appeared in Flyboys, a film about American pilots in the First World War. The film struggled commercially. His work as a producer proved more successful than that early appearance suggested.

He founded Skydance in the same year. The company later worked with established studios on major productions, including films in the Mission Impossible series and Top Gun: Maverick. Producing meant helping assemble the money, people and agreements that made a film possible. Success in that role offered a route towards owning more of the business itself.

In 2025, the Ellison family and investment firm RedBird helped bring Paramount under new control. The acquisition gave the group a famous film studio, the CBS television network, children's programming and a streaming service. Ellison now led a company whose history reached far beyond his own production business. Soon, an even larger opportunity emerged.

A valuable library with bills

Warner Bros. had spent a century building a film and television catalogue. Its characters and stories could earn money through cinemas, television, games, merchandise and streaming. A successful film might attract audiences long after its first release. Owning a library also made it possible to offer subscribers something familiar while new productions were being developed.

Yet a valuable catalogue did not remove financial pressure. Warner had passed through several corporate combinations, including Time Warner and AOL. AT&T acquired Time Warner in 2018, then moved away from its attempt to combine telecommunications with a large entertainment business. In 2022, WarnerMedia joined Discovery. The resulting company carried substantial debt into a changing television market.

For years, cable television had provided dependable income. Households paid for bundles containing many channels, including some they rarely watched. Channels received distribution revenue and sold advertising. This arrangement helped fund expensive programmes and supported large companies with regular cash receipts.

Streaming weakened that model as viewers cancelled traditional subscriptions. Building a streaming service required spending on programmes, technology and marketing, while customers could leave after watching the series they wanted. The established business was shrinking before its replacement had necessarily become equally dependable. Debt payments continued regardless of how audiences chose to watch.

In June 2025, Warner Bros. Discovery announced plans to divide into two listed companies. One would contain studios and streaming, including HBO. The other would contain much of the television network business. The proposed split made the different parts easier to evaluate. It also raised an obvious question for potential buyers: should they acquire the growing attractions, the whole group, or nothing at all?

Two different offers

Netflix pursued the studio and streaming assets. Paramount wanted the whole company. This difference mattered as much as the headline price. An offer for selected businesses could leave shareholders with an interest in the remaining networks and their associated financial obligations. An offer for every share promised a different outcome, with cash replacing the shareholder's ownership of the entire group.

Paramount's early approaches failed to persuade Warner's board. It then took an offer directly to shareholders, trying to win support without the board's recommendation. Such an approach is often described as hostile. The word refers to the relationship with the target's leadership, rather than to anything unlawful about making an offer.

Price alone was not enough. Shareholders also needed confidence that a buyer could obtain the money and complete the transaction. A higher promise could be less attractive if it was unlikely to reach closing. Financing commitments, contractual protections and the cost of abandoning an earlier agreement therefore became part of the contest.

In February 2026, Paramount offered 31 dollars per share. Warner's board judged the proposal superior under its agreement with Netflix. Netflix declined to increase its offer, saying that matching the new price would no longer make financial sense. Losing an auction can be a deliberate decision to protect a business from paying more than it expects to recover.

Where the money came from

The financing plan announced with the agreement included 47 billion dollars in new equity. Investors would receive newly issued shares in exchange for providing capital. These were funds brought into the purchase by investors, rather than profits that Paramount had accumulated from selling cinema tickets or subscriptions.

Banks and other lenders also committed substantial financing. These commitments included arrangements connected with existing obligations as well as additional borrowing. Adding every financing headline together does not produce a simple cash purchase price. Some facilities replace or support other facilities, and the enterprise value already includes debt belonging to the acquired business.

New equity and borrowing create different claims. Shareholders own a portion of the business and accept the risk that their investment may lose value. Lenders expect repayment under agreed terms. Issuing more shares can reduce the proportion owned by existing shareholders. Borrowing avoids that particular effect but creates payments that must be met even in disappointing years.

This is how a smaller company can acquire a larger one. Its current stock market value is not a spending limit. Outside investors can supply capital, while lenders assess the cash the combined business might generate. The buyer gains access to the target's earnings, but it also inherits exposure to its problems.

Control is a separate question. Different classes of shares can carry different voting rights. Someone who contributes a large amount of money may receive a substantial economic interest without gaining equivalent influence over management. Understanding who owns a business therefore requires looking at both the financial stake and the rights attached to it.

After the signatures

Signing the agreement did not immediately transfer the company. Approvals and closing conditions still had to be satisfied. The acquisition was completed on October 6, 2026. That distinction matters whenever a proposed merger appears in the news. A signed contract describes an intended transaction. Closing establishes that it has actually happened.

Management presented the combination as an opportunity to improve production and reduce duplicated costs. Such savings may come from shared systems, offices or distribution. They can also involve difficult decisions about employment and investment. Announced savings are targets, and their eventual size depends on decisions that have yet to produce results.

For viewers, a corporate merger does not automatically combine subscriptions or put every film into one application. Rights agreements, existing services and commercial plans still shape what can be watched. For employees and creators, the consequences may be more immediate as a smaller number of decision makers influence budgets and commissions.

The acquisition brought an extraordinary collection of entertainment businesses together. It also left the new management responsible for making an expensive financial plan work. Films must still find audiences, subscribers must still decide to stay, and lenders must still be paid. Buying a famous name can be completed on a particular day. Earning enough from it remains an ongoing task.

title: Full planes, thin profits
body:
A full aircraft looks like a successful business. Nearly every seat has been sold, passengers have paid for bags, and the crew is preparing to leave. Yet the airline may earn very little from the journey. Once fuel, wages, maintenance and other bills have been paid, only a small part of the money collected may remain. Sometimes the flight loses money despite carrying plenty of people.

That problem became especially visible in 2026. In its June outlook, the International Air Transport Association expected the world's airlines to make a combined net profit of 23 billion dollars. Its earlier forecast had been 41 billion. The revised figure represented a net margin of roughly two percent and about four dollars and fifty cents per passenger. These were industry forecasts, not the final results of every airline or the profit from each individual ticket.

The average concealed large differences. Some companies had stronger finances, better routes or protection against rising fuel prices. Others had entered the year struggling. On May 2, Spirit Airlines announced that it was winding down operations and cancelled its flights. The company cited higher oil prices and other business pressures, and said no additional funding was available. Fuel had worsened an existing financial problem rather than explaining the entire failure on its own.

A seat with an expiry date

An airline sells something it cannot put back on a shelf. Once an aircraft departs, an empty seat on that flight can never be sold. The opportunity has disappeared. This gives airlines a reason to accept lower fares when they expect seats would otherwise remain empty.

But pricing is more complicated than making every ticket cheap. Airlines try to estimate demand, separate different customer needs and decide when to offer lower fares. A passenger booking a holiday months ahead may pay less than someone who needs to travel tomorrow. A busy route with limited competition can support different prices from a route where several airlines compete for the same travellers.

Many costs remain even when bookings disappoint. The aircraft must be financed or leased. Crews must be available, maintenance must be carried out, and airports charge for their services. Carrying another passenger adds some costs, but leaving a seat empty does not remove the airline's main obligations. This is why filling an aircraft can help without guaranteeing a profit.

Revenue figures also need care. Airlines earn money from more than passenger tickets. Cargo, baggage fees and other services contribute to the total. Dividing all industry revenue by the number of passengers does not reveal the average ticket price. It mixes different sources of income into one number, which can make a simple comparison misleading.

Competition changed the business

For much of the twentieth century, governments played a large role in deciding how airlines operated. National carriers connected countries with the wider world. Some routes were important for trade, tourism or public policy even when their direct financial return was weak. Ownership and public support varied between countries, but aviation was often treated as more than an ordinary consumer business.

The United States began a major change with the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978. Economic restrictions on routes and fares were removed over time, giving airlines more freedom to compete. Safety regulation remained. Deregulation did not mean that anyone could simply operate an aircraft wherever they wanted without certification or access to airport facilities.

Competition encouraged cheaper fares and different business models. Airlines focused on costs could attract travellers who had previously found flying too expensive. Established companies had to respond. Passengers gained more opportunities to travel, while airlines faced continuing pressure to offer prices that would cover their costs without sending customers to a rival.

The fuel problem

Fuel is a large expense whose price can change quickly. An airline needs a specific refined product, not simply crude oil. Refinery capacity, transport routes and local availability affect what it pays. A disruption can therefore make jet fuel rise differently from the oil price shown in the evening news.

Conflict and transport disruptions in the Middle East put heavy pressure on fuel markets in 2026.
