The real historical change came after the Taliban returned to power in August 2021. In April 2022, they announced a ban on poppy cultivation and other drug activity. United Nations monitoring subsequently recorded a steep reduction in Afghan cultivation and opium production. Farmers who had relied on the crop faced a serious loss of income.

That decline did not prove that Afghan opium had disappeared permanently. On 29 October 2026, the United Nations reported a substantial rebound in production, although levels remained below those before the ban. The change is a reminder that a market forecast can become outdated. Poverty, enforcement and available alternatives continue to affect what farmers grow.

Why a harvest is not a market

A sudden reduction in production naturally raises questions about supply elsewhere. Afghanistan had long been an important source of the heroin sold in Europe. If less opium was harvested, would heroin become scarcer? And if it did, what would sellers offer instead?

The answer was not immediate. Stored opium could continue to enter the supply chain after fields stopped producing. Traders and suppliers in different places might hold reserves. Other regions might increase production. A change at the beginning of a supply chain does not arrive at every destination at the same time.

The documentary interviews researcher Daniel Brombacher about these uncertainties. He describes efforts to understand whether synthetic opioids already have a market, who buys them and how they are sold. The useful question is not simply whether a feared crisis will happen. It is what evidence can reveal about changes already taking place.

European drug monitoring has treated a shift towards synthetic opioids as a risk requiring preparation, not as an inevitable outcome across the continent. A shortage can create opportunities for substitutes, but markets differ. Buyers, sellers, treatment services and existing drug patterns all affect what follows.

The distinction matters for public communication. Saying that nothing will change may encourage complacency. Saying that a catastrophe is certain can make uncertainty disappear from the story. Neither helps people interpret the evidence. Authorities need to watch changes in availability, composition and harm without pretending to know the future.

An old family of substances

Nitazenes did not begin as a recent invention for online markets. They were developed during pharmaceutical research in the 1950s. They were never approved as medicines. Decades later, members of this family appeared in illicit drug supplies, where quality and contents cannot be assumed from a label.

The name covers different substances, not one uniform drug. Some can match or exceed the potency of fentanyl. A single comparison cannot describe every nitazene, every mixture or every person exposed to it. Dramatic claims about one quantity being able to kill a city obscure these differences rather than explain them.

The central health danger is easier to state. Like other opioids, nitazenes can suppress breathing. Severe poisoning can be fatal. A person who does not know an opioid is present may also have no tolerance to its effects. Uncertainty about the contents makes it harder to recognise the risk before an emergency occurs.

This is why the appearance of a tablet is a poor guide to safety. A counterfeit can resemble a familiar prescription medicine without containing the expected ingredient or a reliable amount of it. The familiarity of the shape or name does not establish how it was manufactured.

European reports have described nitazenes in products sold as heroin and in counterfeit medicines resembling opioid painkillers or sedatives. These are not all the same audience. Some people knowingly seek an opioid. Others believe they have obtained a different drug. Warnings that address only the first group can miss people in the second.

The screen and the parcel

The documentary examines the role of online selling. Its team reports contacting a seller but stopping before completing a purchase. That illustrates an attempted transaction, not laboratory confirmation of a product that arrived. A seller's claim is not proof of a parcel's contents.

There is no need to repeat the purchasing process to understand the concern. Online contact can connect buyers and sellers who never meet. The eventual physical delivery may be only one part of a relationship conducted through messages. That can make the people involved less visible to services accustomed to working in established local drug scenes.

Synthetic production also differs from agriculture. It does not depend on a poppy harvest in the same way as heroin production does. That difference can create commercial incentives for illicit suppliers. It does not mean that production is effortless, that every transaction takes place online or that all sellers will inevitably abandon other drugs.

The documentary contrasts these markets with longer supply chains involving farmers, processors, importers and local dealers. The comparison helps explain why one policing approach may not fit every substance. But real markets can combine different routes and intermediaries. A simple diagram should not be mistaken for a complete map.

For prevention, the question becomes how to reach someone who does not think of themselves as an opioid user. A warning delivered at a local service may never reach a person ordering what they believe is a sedative. That is a challenge for communication, not proof that communication is useless.

What the figures can miss

European monitoring has reported serious harm from nitazenes, with particular concern in the Baltic countries. Yet a list of deaths from different countries can mislead if the years, testing methods and definitions do not match. A small recorded number is not automatically a complete count.

Laboratories must know what they are looking for and use methods capable of detecting it. New substances can be missed by procedures designed for older drugs. This creates a problem for both an individual investigation and the broader picture. If a substance is not identified, the warning signal may be weaker than the actual harm.

A negative test for one substance is not a guarantee about everything else. Fentanyl test strips, for example, do not establish whether nitazenes are absent. Even when a sample is analysed, the result has limits. It should not be turned into a promise that using an illicit product is safe.

Seizure figures require care too. They tell us what authorities found, which depends partly on enforcement priorities and detection. They do not directly reveal the total amount consumed or every route used. An increase can reflect a changing market, improved detection or both.

Better information depends on connections between laboratories, emergency services, treatment providers and warning systems. An unusual poisoning seen in one place may matter elsewhere. Sharing a useful alert quickly can be more valuable than waiting until the problem is large enough to dominate the news.

Treatment still matters

One claim in the original account needs a clear correction. Naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose involving nitazenes. It should not be described as an antidote that works for heroin and fentanyl but fails against this family of substances. Public health guidance includes nitazenes among the opioids for which naloxone is used.

Some emergencies may require repeated doses. That does not make the medicine pointless. It means that an apparent response must not be confused with the end of the emergency. Breathing problems can return, and medical help remains essential. The appropriate response is urgent assistance, not an attempt to identify the exact molecule before acting.

If someone is unresponsive or is not breathing normally, call emergency services immediately. Use available naloxone according to its instructions and follow the dispatcher's guidance. Stay with the person until help arrives. These basic actions belong alongside the discussion of markets because a warning is more useful when people know that help can make a difference.

Access to naloxone and treatment varies between places. Rules about supplying a medicine, local services and practical availability are separate issues. A country may permit an intervention without making it easy for everyone who needs it to obtain it. That gap deserves attention without relying on an outdated list of national rules.

People living with dependence also need more than an emergency response. Treatment, reliable contact with health services and support without humiliation can create opportunities to reduce harm. None of these measures guarantees an outcome. Together, they offer more than waiting for the next arrest or poisoning report.

Before the next warning

The story began with a partner finding someone unconscious at home. The documentary's account gives that danger a personal setting. The broader evidence shows why the concern cannot be confined to one person, one country or one kind of drug buyer.

Afghan farming, synthetic substances and online markets are connected, but they do not form a single inevitable sequence. A harvest can fall and later recover. A seller can change products. A laboratory can identify a substance that earlier tests missed. Preparation depends on noticing those changes and responding to what they show.

The practical work is often less dramatic than the headlines: updating testing, sharing alerts, making treatment accessible and helping people recognise an overdose. It also means speaking clearly about uncertainty. A familiar tablet may not contain a familiar medicine, and an apparently small market can still cause devastating harm.

The aim is not to make every reader memorise a catalogue of chemicals. It is to make an unfamiliar risk understandable before another household encounters it without warning. Behind the statistics are people who can still be reached, treated and helped.

title: The state sells cigarettes
body:
A company behind the counter

A cigarette packet usually carries a brand name, not a diagram of the institutions behind it. A customer sees a colour, a logo and a familiar product. In China, many apparently separate cigarette brands lead back to the same enormous business: China National Tobacco Corporation, often called China Tobacco.

Outside its home market, the name attracts less attention than many international consumer brands. Yet the company occupies a central position in a country with a vast cigarette market. Its importance goes beyond factories and sales. It is closely tied to the state institutions that oversee the industry, while tobacco generates substantial public revenue.

That arrangement creates the central problem explored by the documentary. A government has a responsibility to protect health. It also receives money from products that cause serious disease. When commercial and regulatory roles are closely connected, a policy that protects people can threaten an important source of income.

The tension does not mean every official has the same priorities. Health workers, researchers and people trying to stop smoking have their own interests and experiences. It does mean that the debate takes place within an unequal structure, where the producer has influence far beyond an ordinary shop counter.

Machines and a larger market

The history begins well before the modern Chinese monopoly. In the nineteenth century, cigarette production depended heavily on workers rolling tobacco by hand. Making more cigarettes meant employing more skilled workers. Machinery changed the scale of the business.

In 1884, the Duke company installed Bonsack cigarette machines at its factory in Durham, North Carolina. The equipment was imperfect, and mechanic William T. O'Brien helped improve it. Once the machines worked more reliably, production costs fell. James B. Duke combined the new manufacturing capacity with aggressive advertising.

This was not merely a faster way to make an existing product. Cheap mass production gave manufacturers a reason to seek much larger markets. Advertising and distribution became crucial companions to the machine. Producing enormous quantities mattered commercially only if people could be persuaded to buy them.

The documentary follows that expansion towards China. Foreign tobacco interests became powerful there before the Communist victory in 1949. During the following years, cigarette factories came under state control. The ownership changed, but the product had already become established in everyday life.

In the early 1980s, the national tobacco corporation brought the state's tobacco interests into a more coordinated structure. The result was a business with reach across production and distribution. Its scale came from a large domestic market and from the institutional arrangements that protected its position within that market.

Two roles under one roof

China Tobacco's relationship with the State Tobacco Monopoly Administration is essential to understanding the system. The commercial corporation and the monopoly administration have closely connected leadership and operations. The administration's responsibilities include overseeing parts of the tobacco supply chain. It is not an independent health authority standing outside the business it regulates.

This creates practical questions. Who decides which interests receive priority when a proposed restriction might reduce sales? How much influence should a producer have over rules governing its products? Can officials responsible for commercial performance also be expected to welcome measures that make smoking less attractive?

The documentary describes the industry as extending from tobacco cultivation through processing and cigarette manufacture to sales and trade. The connections matter because a proposed change does not affect only one factory. It can touch local employment, suppliers, retailers and public budgets. Those relationships can make reform politically difficult even when the health evidence is clear.

The money is substantial, but accounting language matters. Taxes, company profits and contributions to public finances are related quantities, not interchangeable ones. Adding taxes and profits together and comparing the result with another company's profit alone does not produce a fair comparison. Nor does a large fiscal contribution prove that smoking creates a net benefit for society.

Illness has costs that do not appear beside cigarette receipts. A family can lose earnings when someone becomes too ill to work. Treatment takes time and money. Premature death changes households in ways that a revenue total cannot describe. The public debate needs to consider those costs as well as the money collected from sales.

Putting a number on the harm

The documentary draws on reporting by The Examination, which published a striking estimate in May 2026. Its analysis attributed about 57 million deaths between 1990 and 2023 to China Tobacco's products. That figure was a calculation based on mortality modelling and market share, not a list of individually verified deaths caused by one company.

The analysis used estimates from the Global Burden of Disease project, led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation. It took a lower estimate of tobacco related deaths in China, including harm from other people's smoke, and applied the company's dominant market share. It also discussed uncertainty and criticism of the underlying mortality estimates.

The distinction does not make tobacco harmless. It explains what the number can and cannot establish. A model can reveal the likely scale of a public health burden without identifying the manufacturer responsible for every individual illness. The corporate attribution is the news organisation's analysis, not a direct WHO finding or a judicial verdict.

Long delays also complicate the picture. The cigarette sold today and a diagnosis made today do not necessarily belong to the same period of exposure. Diseases can develop after years of smoking. A company can continue to be associated with severe harm even while smoking becomes less common among younger people.

The point of examining the producer is not to blame people who have become dependent on nicotine. It is to ask who designs, distributes and promotes the product, who earns money from it, and who has the power to change the conditions in which it is sold.

A promise and its implementation

China ratified the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in October 2005. It entered into force for China in January 2006. The country is the treaty party, not the tobacco corporation. That distinction matters because the responsibility to implement public health commitments belongs to the state.

The treaty addresses areas such as exposure to tobacco smoke, advertising and information on packaging. Its obligations and accompanying guidance should not be collapsed into the claim that every country must use an identical packet design. The broader issue is whether measures give people meaningful protection and clear information.

Investigative reporting has described resistance to reform. In a 2023 investigation, The Examination reported that China Tobacco had influenced the implementation of tobacco controls, including local rules. It described a 2020 smoking law in Chongqing that allowed designated smoking areas in several types of venues after company leaders met local officials. The reporting attributed influence to the monopoly, rather than establishing a criminal judgment.

The same investigation reported that the company had worked to weaken treaty language and policy measures. China Tobacco and the Chinese government did not respond to the reporters' questions, according to the publication. Their silence is not an admission. The findings remain attributed reporting, while the underlying institutional conflict can be examined in its own right.

The packet as a message

Packaging is a small object with a large communication role. Colours, symbols and the arrangement of a brand name can suggest quality, tradition or status. The documentary describes cigarettes given as gifts and offered during social occasions. These practices exist, but they do not mean every person in China welcomes a cigarette or regards refusal as rude.

A health warning competes with those messages. A brief general sentence may communicate less than a clear explanation of a specific harm. Large warnings and restrictions on branding are intended to reduce the ability of a packet to advertise the product. Their effect should be assessed through evidence, rather than a dramatic claim that one design change alone made an exact number of people quit.

Another message can appear scientific: a lower tar figure. Someone worried about health may interpret it as evidence that one cigarette is safer than another. But the number can come from a smoking machine, which does not behave like a human being. It is not a reliable measure of what an individual will inhale.

The National Cancer Institute explains that cigarettes marketed as light or low tar are not safer than ordinary cigarettes. Changes in how a person smokes can undermine the apparent reduction measured by a machine. A reassuring description on a packet does not remove the risks of cancer and other disease.

This is where information and commercial incentives meet. A customer may want reassurance rather than a reason to stop. A producer may benefit when concern leads to switching brands instead of leaving the market. Public health communication needs to address that misunderstanding without treating the customer as foolish for believing a seemingly technical claim.

Change is already happening

The original documentary makes the sweeping claim that smoking has declined almost everywhere except China. More recent national survey evidence does not support that wording. China's survey found current smoking among people aged fifteen and older fell from 26.6 percent in 2018 to 23.2 percent in 2024.

The decline is real progress, although the remaining burden is large. The same 2024 survey found a substantial difference between men and women. A single national average therefore conceals very different patterns. It also should not be confused with the percentage of the entire population, including young children.

Falling prevalence and continued commercial power can exist together. So can fewer smokers and serious illness caused by past exposure. These are different measurements. Understanding them prevents a false choice between declaring the problem solved and insisting that nothing has improved.

State ownership alone does not explain every country's smoking pattern. Private tobacco companies have also resisted restrictions and promoted misleading claims. The relevant questions concern the strength of health policy, the independence of decisions, commercial influence and access to help for people who want to stop.

The future is not fixed by the size of the company. Institutions can change priorities, clearer warnings can challenge familiar assumptions, and fewer young people can begin smoking. None of that happens automatically. It requires decisions that place preventable illness beside revenue when judging the industry's role.

At the shop counter, the product still looks small. A packet fits in a pocket and a purchase takes only a moment. Behind it stand factories, public institutions and years of health consequences. Seeing those connections makes the story larger than a choice between brands. It becomes a question of what a state is prepared to protect when the product it sells harms the people it serves.

title: After the cartel leader
body:
The operation in Tapalpa

On 22 February 2026, Mexican authorities announced that they had finally reached the man they had pursued for years. Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, better known as El Mencho, had been found in Tapalpa, in the western state of Jalisco. He led the Cártel Jalisco Nueva Generación, usually shortened to CJNG.

According to Mexico's defence ministry, troops met armed resistance during an operation intended to capture him. Several people were killed. El Mencho was wounded and died while being transported by air. The first announcement still left formal identification to forensic specialists. Days later, the authorities released his body to relatives after genetic checks.

The news seemed to offer a clear ending. A powerful criminal leader had escaped arrest for years, and now he was dead. But the violence that followed made that ending much less convincing. Vehicles burned, roads were blocked and people across several states faced sudden danger. A leader was gone. The organization associated with his name could still act.

To understand that apparent contradiction, it helps to look beyond the hunt for one man. CJNG had grown through relationships with local groups, access to illegal markets and the ability to frighten people into obedience. Those relationships did not all depend on El Mencho being physically present. His death raised an urgent question about who would take charge, but also a harder one about what would happen to the people living under the cartel's influence.

From an older organization

CJNG did not appear in an empty criminal market. It emerged around 2010 and 2011 from the remains of the Milenio cartel, an organization that had been associated with Sinaloa. Arrests and internal divisions had weakened the older group. Members reorganized, formed new alliances and fought over what remained.

The dates vary slightly between accounts because the creation of a cartel is rarely a single event. There is no public opening ceremony or reliable register of its first members. A name may become visible after the people behind it have already been working together. What matters here is the continuity. CJNG inherited connections and experience from an existing criminal world.

Under El Mencho, it became an independent force and eventually a major rival to Sinaloa. Jalisco gave the group its name, but its reach expanded beyond that state. Researchers at ACLED have documented the growth of CJNG and affiliated groups across central and western Mexico, along with violent struggles over territory.

Maps of cartel influence can make this look simpler than it is. A coloured area might suggest that one organization controls every road, town and business within it. In practice, the presence of an armed group can vary from one place to another. Rivals may operate nearby, local alliances may change, and residents may face pressure from more than one group. A map records an assessment of influence, not a stable border between countries.

That distinction also matters when describing the cartel's size. A large network can be dangerous without being perfectly united. Its members may share an enemy or a source of income while disagreeing about who should lead them. Expansion creates opportunities for a criminal organization, but it also brings people whose loyalty may depend on circumstances.

A name with many branches

Analysts sometimes describe CJNG as a franchise. The comparison refers to smaller groups joining a wider organization while continuing to operate locally. It can help explain how a cartel spreads without sending its central leadership to manage every town.

It should not be taken too literally. A criminal network is not a chain of ordinary shops with a public contract and identical rules. Local commanders have their own contacts, interests and histories. Relationships can involve cooperation, coercion or both. The same name does not prove that every action has been ordered personally by one leader.

For residents, however, uncertainty about the command structure offers little comfort. A threat can still change how someone travels, works or spends money. A business owner does not need to know the identity of every superior in the organization to fear the person making demands at the door. The pressure is immediate even when the wider network is difficult to see.

This is why the language of business success can become misleading. Describing a cartel as efficient or innovative may explain part of its organization, but it can also make violence sound like a management technique with no victims. Its income depends on crimes, and its influence can depend on people believing that refusal will bring punishment.

The central leader still matters. He may settle disputes, maintain relationships and give the organization a recognizable identity. But those functions are different from personally controlling every transaction. The more work is carried out through regional figures and associates, the more there is to investigate beyond the person whose photograph appears on a wanted poster.

More than one source of money

Drug trafficking was central to CJNG's rise. Methamphetamine became an important part of its business, alongside cocaine and later illicit fentanyl. The markets reached beyond Mexico. The damage did too, extending to people who used the drugs and to families dealing with dependence, illness and death.

The cartel also developed sources of income outside the drug trade. ACLED has described activities including extortion, kidnapping and fuel theft. These businesses connect organized crime to people who may have no involvement with drugs at all. Someone can be affected because of where they live, what they grow or the business they run.

One example attracted an official warning in July 2024. FinCEN, the FBI and the US Treasury's sanctions office highlighted fraud associated with Mexican criminal organizations, including CJNG, targeting American owners of timeshares in Mexico. A timeshare gives someone the right to use holiday accommodation for an agreed period. The warning concerned fraud against owners, rather than simply a bad holiday rental.

The distinction matters because it shows how misleading the familiar image of a drug cartel can be. Victims may encounter an apparently commercial proposal and never meet an armed person. The crime can reach across a border through a financial relationship. Its connection to a violent organization may only become clear later.

Having several sources of money can also make an organization harder to dismantle. Interrupting one business does not automatically remove the others. This does not mean every cartel activity succeeds or that enforcement is pointless. It means investigators need to establish how particular people and businesses are connected, rather than assume that one seizure has stopped the whole network.

Fear and public image

The documentary behind this story describes CJNG presenting itself as a protector while using threats and violence. Such a claim deserves scrutiny. A group can denounce a rival's crimes without giving up its own. Public displays of generosity do not establish that the people watching are free to reject the giver.

The same problem applies to images circulated online. A recording can show armed men, expensive possessions or a crowd gathered at an event. It cannot, by itself, show how freely everyone participated or how representative the scene is. Treating a cartel's publicity as a transparent account of local life gives the organization too much control over the story.

Some of the clearest evidence of CJNG's violence came through criminal proceedings. On 1 May 2015, its members shot down a Mexican armed forces helicopter. At least nine people aboard died. In a later US prosecution, evidence attributed the order to El Mencho's son, Rubén Oseguera González, known as El Menchito.

The similar nicknames can cause confusion, but father and son were separate people with separate responsibilities. In September 2024, a federal jury convicted El Menchito of drug trafficking conspiracy and firearms offences. In March 2025, he received a sentence of life imprisonment plus thirty years. The account of the helicopter attack formed part of the evidence described by the US Justice Department.

That record is more useful than an unsupported claim that one cartel caused a precise share of all killings in Mexico. A national homicide total cannot simply be assigned to a single organization. Serious crimes do not become less serious when a writer refuses to attach an unverified number to them. The people who died in the helicopter were enough reason to investigate and prosecute those responsible.

What an operation can achieve

In March 2020, US authorities announced the results of Project Python, an operation targeting CJNG. Over six months, it had produced more than six hundred arrests and three hundred and fifty indictments. Those were different measures. An arrest was not a conviction, and an indictment was a formal accusation that still had to be tested through the legal process.

The figures showed a substantial enforcement effort. They did not establish that the cartel had disappeared. When an organization continues to operate after arrests, it is tempting to call the whole operation a failure. That conclusion asks too much of a single headline. Removing particular offenders and building cases against them can matter even when others remain active.

The opposite conclusion would be premature as well. A large number of arrests does not prove that residents are safer or that an organization has lost the ability to replace people. Assessing the outcome requires looking at what happens afterwards, including whether criminal activity moves, whether new leaders emerge and whether threats against communities decline.

There is a question of whose experience gets counted. An official report may describe the number of suspects detained, while a resident wants to know whether it is safe to report a threat. Both concern the same operation, but they measure different things. A convincing account of progress needs evidence about the second question as well as the first.

CJNG's own origins illustrate the difficulty. It emerged after an older organization had weakened and divided. That history does not mean authorities should leave violent leaders alone. It does show why capturing a leader and preventing a successor organization are different tasks. Courts can punish an individual. Sustained protection for communities requires work beyond that individual's case.

International measures added another layer. In February 2025, the United States designated CJNG a foreign terrorist organization. This was a US legal designation with specific consequences, not a finding that every allegation about everyone linked to the cartel had been proved. Criminal responsibility still required attention to particular people, conduct and evidence.

After El Mencho

The February 2026 operation brought years of pursuit to a close. Mexican authorities said American information had contributed to the effort. That account described a Mexican operation with supplementary US intelligence, rather than an American ground assault. The distinction was important amid debate about how far the United States might intervene against cartels.

The retaliatory violence then exposed the gap between removing a leader and securing the places affected by his organization. For someone facing a blocked road or a burning vehicle nearby, the immediate issue was getting home safely. A major announcement from the government could coexist with fear in the streets.

It was too early in the first days to know how leadership would settle. Later information changed that picture. On 23 July 2026, the US Treasury identified Juan Carlos Gonzalez, also known as Juan Carlos Valencia Gonzalez and Pelon, as CJNG's new leader. Treasury described him as El Mencho's stepson and a longtime member of the organization.

This was a dated assessment by US authorities. It gave a more current answer than simply saying there was no known successor, while leaving room for uncertainty about how authority worked across different local groups. Identifying a leader is not the same as observing every relationship inside a secretive organization.

The history of CJNG leaves no neat final scene. El Mencho's death was a major event, and the prosecution of his son brought a serious criminal case to judgment. Neither event erased the connections through which the organization earned money and exercised force. Those connections remained the subject of investigations and sanctions.

For the people living with cartel violence, the useful measure of change is less dramatic than the fall of a famous boss. It is whether a shop can stay open without threats, whether a journey can be made safely and whether a witness can speak without fearing retaliation. Those are ordinary expectations. Making them dependable is the unfinished work that remains after the cameras leave.

title: Peter Thiel and power
body:
A question about freedom

In 2009, Peter Thiel published an essay with a sentence that would follow him for years: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” It was a striking statement from a businessman whose career had benefited from American universities, financial markets and legal institutions. He was not an obscure commentator. He had helped build PayPal, invested in Facebook and become involved in a company supplying software to government agencies.

Thiel's idea of freedom placed great importance on individuals being able to build, invest and experiment without political interference. Democracy, however, gives other people a say in the rules that govern those activities. The tension between those two positions runs through his public career.

It would be easy to turn that career into a story about one man secretly moving every piece on a chessboard. Thiel does play chess, and the comparison appears often in accounts of his life. But influence is not the same as complete control. Businesses fail, political allies disagree, and institutions can resist the wishes of their richest participants. The more useful question is how his money, ideas and relationships have given him opportunities that most people never have.

The student newspaper

At Stanford, Thiel helped create a place for arguments that he felt were missing from campus debate. In 1987, he became the first editor of the Stanford Review. The paper challenged the prevailing politics of the university and developed a reputation for provocation. Its own history describes a founding mission of presenting alternative viewpoints.

The newspaper also brought people together. A publication needs writers, editors and readers who return for the next issue. Over time, those relationships can outlast the arguments that first created them. In Thiel's later career, connections made through education and work would become part of a much wider business and political network.

Accounts of his student years often try to explain his politics through his childhood or his treatment by classmates. Such explanations can sound convincing without being easy to prove. A person's later beliefs cannot be read directly from a school experience. What is visible is that Thiel was already interested in challenging campus orthodoxies and organizing people who shared some of his objections.

He completed his undergraduate degree at Stanford in 1989 and his law degree in 1992. For a time, he followed a conventional professional path into legal work. It did not hold his attention. In a later Stanford appearance, he described a law firm where outsiders wanted to get in and the people inside wanted to leave. He eventually turned toward investing and technology.

Money moving online

In the late 1990s, online shopping created a practical problem. Buyers and sellers needed a way to transfer money quickly, including when they did not already have a relationship. Thiel and the engineer Max Levchin became involved in building a business that would help solve it. That business became PayPal.

The product was useful for a simple reason. A payment could connect people who were otherwise separated by distance and unfamiliar banking arrangements. But moving money also created difficult responsibilities. Fraud, losses and disputes did not disappear because a transaction happened on a screen. A service that made payment easier also needed ways to handle people using it dishonestly.

PayPal's development included competition and a merger with X.com, the company associated with Elon Musk. The history contains disagreements about management and technology, but the broad outcome is clear. Thiel became chief executive of the combined business, and PayPal established itself in online commerce.

On 3 October 2002, eBay completed its purchase of PayPal. The announced transaction value was approximately $1.5 billion, paid through an exchange of shares. It was not a cash payment of that amount to Thiel. He resigned as chief executive when the deal closed. The sale nevertheless gave him capital and a business record that made future founders more likely to take his calls.

In his later political writing, Thiel described a founding ambition for PayPal that went beyond convenient payments. He had imagined money escaping government control. The actual company still operated within a world of banks, customers, contracts and regulators. The distance between the ambition and the operating business would recur in other projects.

The value of an early bet

Thiel became an early investor in Facebook, supporting a company that was still far from the global platform it would become. He also served on its board for many years. When Meta announced his planned departure in 2022, Mark Zuckerberg publicly credited him with advice on business and economics as well as early belief in the company.

An investment can therefore buy more than a financial interest. It can establish a relationship at a moment when a founder needs money and reassurance. Advice given during those early years may influence later decisions. That does not mean an investor makes every decision, but it helps explain why a comparatively small group of people can appear repeatedly in the histories of large technology companies.

Thiel has also argued that entrepreneurs should try to create businesses with something distinctive enough to escape ordinary competition. In a Stanford discussion of his ideas, he described monopoly as a goal for a company. His argument was that intense rivalry can trap businesses in small differences while a genuinely new product creates a market of its own.

There is a harder question on the other side of that argument. A powerful company may offer a valuable service while leaving customers, workers or competitors with fewer alternatives. Business success and public benefit do not always move together. Judging a company requires looking at what it does with its position, not merely how cleverly it acquired it.

Software for the state

Palantir brought Thiel's business interests into especially close contact with public power. Founded in 2003 by a team that included Thiel, the company developed software for working with complex information. Alex Karp, another figure from his Stanford connections, became its chief executive.

The name comes from the seeing stones in Tolkien's fiction. That reference is memorable, but it can also encourage an exaggerated picture of the technology. Palantir does not possess a magical view of everything happening in the world. Its software helps users bring information together, examine relationships and organize work. What users can establish depends on the information available, its quality and the decisions people make with it.

For an investigator, connecting records may reveal a relationship that was difficult to see when the records were kept separately. The same process can also carry mistakes from one system into another. A misspelled name, an outdated record or a misleading association can matter greatly if the result affects someone's freedom. Technical capability and justified conclusions are different things.

Government customers make those questions particularly important. Public agencies can investigate, detain and use force in ways that ordinary businesses cannot. A private company supplying them with software becomes part of how public authority works, even when officials remain responsible for the decisions.

An ICE procurement document from April 2025 illustrates the relationship. It described Palantir's existing case management software and proposed ImmigrationOS capabilities for immigration enforcement. The agency wanted to connect records and support operational workflows using infrastructure it already had. This was a concrete administrative role, not evidence that the software could reliably predict what every person would do next.

The document also helps explain why an established supplier can be difficult to replace. Once software has been configured around an agency's records and procedures, switching to another provider takes time. That creates a practical dependence worth examining separately from any claim about a personal relationship between an investor and a politician.

Military work raises additional questions. Palantir has acknowledged work with Israel's defence establishment after the attacks of 7 October 2023. It has also explicitly denied providing or being involved in the systems known as Gospel and Lavender. Those denials need to remain visible when discussing allegations about targeting technology. Neither the existence of a defence contract nor a company's denial of a specific allegation establishes everything its software does in a conflict.

The public does not see every detail of such work. That limited visibility makes careful distinctions more necessary. It does not justify treating a company as all powerful, and it does not remove the need to examine contracts, safeguards and the effects on people whose information is processed.

A courtroom and a publisher

Thiel's influence became visible in another setting through the case against Gawker Media. In 2012, Gawker published intimate footage of the wrestler Hulk Hogan. Hogan sued over the invasion of his privacy. Thiel helped finance the litigation, a role that became public after the trial.

In 2016, a jury awarded Hogan $140 million. The parties later reached a $31 million settlement, and Gawker had entered bankruptcy. The distinction between the verdict and the settlement matters. The original award was not simply the amount ultimately paid.

Thiel had his own history with Gawker, which had publicly discussed his sexuality in 2007. He described his support for litigation as a response to reporting that harmed people without serving a public interest. That was his explanation for his involvement, rather than proof of every private motive attributed to him.

The case brought two legitimate concerns into conflict. Publication of intimate material can violate privacy even when the person involved is famous. At the same time, a wealthy individual funding a case against a critical publisher can create a chilling effect beyond that particular dispute. Other editors may wonder whether investigating a rich person will expose them to legal costs they cannot survive.

Freedom House discussed those concerns in its account of internet freedom in 2016. The issue was not that publishers should have immunity from the law. It was that access to legal resources is deeply unequal. The ability to finance litigation can shape which disputes reach court and how long the parties can afford to continue.

An argument against politics

Thiel's 2009 essay had already made his frustration with electoral politics explicit. He identified women voters and recipients of welfare as groups resistant to libertarian policies. In a clarification appended to the essay, he said he did not think any group should lose the vote. That qualification belongs beside his criticism, rather than disappearing from the account.

He suggested looking for freedom through new spaces created by technology, including the internet, ocean settlements and eventually space. The idea was that a builder might create possibilities without first winning an election. But a project can offer new choices while still raising questions about the people affected by it. A place governed under unusual rules must still decide who writes those rules and who can challenge them.

Libertarianism itself includes different positions. Wanting lower taxes or fewer restrictions on business does not automatically mean rejecting democracy. Thiel's particular criticism should be understood as his argument, not assigned to everyone who uses the same political label.

Entering the political arena

Despite his frustration with politics, Thiel continued participating in it. In July 2016, he spoke at the Republican National Convention in support of Donald Trump. His appearance was public and deliberate. He presented himself as someone who built companies and argued that the prosperity of Silicon Valley had not reached much of the country.

The speech showed how a business reputation could become a political resource. An investor known for backing successful companies could tell an audience that he saw promise in a candidate too. That was an endorsement, not a guarantee that the candidate would deliver the investor's preferred policies.

Thiel later provided major financial support to an outside political organization backing J. D. Vance's Senate bid. In 2022, the Washington Post reported that he had given $15 million to a super PAC supporting Vance. The money went to an outside group, not directly to Vance's campaign.

That distinction does not make the support unimportant. Money can help a candidate become visible and remain competitive. But it also does not establish that the donor controls the candidate or that voters played no role. Vance won a Senate seat and later joined Trump's presidential ticket. After the 2024 election, he took office as vice president on 20 January 2025.

These connections deserve scrutiny because they place people with longstanding business ties near public decisions. Scrutiny is different from assuming that every policy is purchased. A useful investigation asks what was donated, who received it, what decisions followed and what evidence links them. A photograph of two people together cannot answer all of those questions.

Different rules, familiar institutions

Projects associated with Thiel have often explored ways to change the conditions under which people live and work. Some involve new technology. Others involve governance, finance or attempts to extend human life. The ambitions can be large, but an ambition is not the same as a demonstrated result. Research into aging has not made human beings immortal.

Erebor, a banking venture he has backed, provides a useful example of the distance between a dramatic description and the institutional reality. Calling it a crypto bank can suggest a project outside the financial system. Yet in October 2025, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted preliminary conditional approval for its national bank charter. In December, the FDIC approved its deposit insurance application subject to conditions.

The proposed business covered technology and other industries, including participants in virtual currency markets. Those approvals were steps within a regulatory process. They did not create a bank beyond government oversight. In this case, innovation was being pursued through public institutions with legal requirements attached.

Próspera in Honduras raises a different set of questions about private development and government authority. The project has become associated with debate over special rules for investment and governance. It is not an independent country free of all law. A dispute between the investors and Honduras has been proceeding through international arbitration.

As of October 2026, the public ICSID case record listed that proceeding as pending. The existence of a claim did not mean the investors had won, and the dispute itself showed how contested the arrangement was. It would be misleading to present the project as a completed political experiment whose future had already been settled.

Who gets to decide?

Thiel's career moves between several kinds of power. A newspaper can shape an argument. An investment can give a company room to grow. Software can change how an agency works. Funding can help sustain a political campaign or a lawsuit. These are different mechanisms, and each creates its own questions about responsibility.

His supporters see an investor willing to take unusual ideas seriously and support people whom others overlook. Critics see concentrated wealth giving one person an outsized role in decisions with consequences far beyond his own life. Both descriptions point toward something that can be examined through actual choices, institutions and outcomes.

There is no need to imagine a secret plan that explains every event. The public record already presents a difficult question. When a wealthy builder wants freedom from rules, what happens to the freedom of people who must live with what he builds? Their ability to understand, challenge and change those arrangements is part of the story too.

title: Who shapes our sweet tooth?
body:
Breakfast and the bigger picture

Imagine a breakfast table with crunchy cereal, milk, toast, jam and a glass of juice. Nothing looks unusual. There is no bowl of sweets in the middle of the table. Yet several of the foods may contain substantial amounts of sugar. How much depends on the products and portions. Working out what that means for health takes more than adding every number on the packets together.

Milk contains naturally occurring sugar. So does fruit. Sugar can also be added during manufacturing, cooking or at the table. These categories matter because health recommendations do not treat every food containing sugar as interchangeable. An apple, a glass of juice and a bottle of lemonade have different structures and nutritional qualities, even when some of their sugars are chemically similar.

The World Health Organization recommends keeping free sugars below ten percent of total energy intake. It conditionally recommends a further reduction below five percent for additional benefits. For an illustrative daily intake of two thousand calories, those figures correspond to fifty and twenty five grams. They are not universal limits on all sugar for every person.

Free sugars include sugar added to food and drinks, as well as sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice. They do not include the sugars naturally present inside intact fruit or in milk. A breakfast calculation that includes all the sugar in plain milk and compares it with the lower free sugar recommendation therefore mixes different measures.

The distinction does not make the problem disappear. It makes it easier to describe accurately. Sweetened drinks and familiar packaged foods can make free sugars easy to consume throughout the day. The question is why reducing that intake has proved so difficult, even when public health organizations have been calling for action for years.

What sweetness does and does not explain

Sweet foods can be pleasurable. They can also be convenient, cheap and available when people are tired or in a hurry. It is tempting to explain every choice through an ancient instinct that modern industry has learned to exploit. Human preferences do have a biological history, but a story about a prehistoric person discovering berries cannot explain the whole modern food system.

Price, advertising, habit and the products available nearby all influence what people buy. A parent choosing food after a long working day is making a decision within those conditions. Describing the result as nothing more than weak willpower leaves most of the situation out of view.

The body uses glucose, but people do not need to obtain it by adding table sugar to meals or drinking sweetened beverages. Many foods supply carbohydrates, and the body has ways of maintaining its glucose supply. That does not mean every sweet food is forbidden. It means the nutritional need for glucose is not an argument for adding sugar without limit.

There are good reasons to pay particular attention to drinks. They can provide substantial energy without the same eating experience as a solid meal. A person may drink something sweet alongside food rather than instead of it. Over time, choices that increase energy intake can contribute to weight gain, although weight is influenced by many factors.

Dental health is another concern. Frequent exposure to free sugars supports processes that cause tooth decay. Brushing matters, but it does not make diet irrelevant. Nor should a discussion of diet imply that dental care is unnecessary. Different preventive measures address different parts of the problem.

Type 2 diabetes is more complicated than the claim that people get it because they eat sugar. Insulin resistance, genes, activity, age and other factors contribute to risk. People should not be blamed for a diagnosis, and type 1 diabetes should not be confused with this discussion. A disease can have preventable risk factors without every case being preventable by an individual's choices.

A systematic review published in the BMJ in 2015 found that higher consumption of sweetened beverages was associated with a higher incidence of type 2 diabetes, including after adjustment for body fatness. It combined prospective observational studies. That supports concern, but it is different from an experiment proving that one extra drink causes a particular person to develop diabetes.

Claims about sugar causing every kind of cancer, dementia or mental illness go beyond what such evidence establishes. Health arguments become weaker when several different diseases are bundled together as if the evidence were identical. The case for reducing excessive free sugar consumption does not require that exaggeration.

Following the money into research

The debate also has a history of commercial influence. In the United States during the 1960s, researchers were examining possible dietary contributors to heart disease. Sugar, fat and cholesterol were all part of the discussion. For the sugar industry, the direction of that discussion had financial consequences.

Decades later, historians of health research examined internal industry documents. Their 2016 analysis described how the Sugar Research Foundation financed a literature review involving Harvard researchers D. Mark Hegsted, Robert McGandy and Frederick Stare. The project was known internally as Project 226. The resulting review appeared in two parts in 1967.

These were not two new clinical experiments. They were an assessment of existing research. According to the historical analysis, the review gave greater weight to fat and cholesterol while discounting evidence concerning sugar. The industry funding was not disclosed in the publication. Disclosure requirements at the time differed from today's, but readers still lacked information that would have helped them assess the relationship.

This history does not prove that every conclusion about saturated fat was wrong. It shows how a sponsor can influence which questions receive attention and how existing evidence is presented. A choice about emphasis can matter without anyone inventing a laboratory result.

Another project, known as Project 259, involved animal research in Britain. A later examination of industry records described work on sugar, intestinal microbes and blood fats, along with findings concerning an enzyme previously associated with bladder cancer. Funding ended, and the historians did not find published results from the project.

Those findings should not be turned into a claim that researchers had proved sugar causes bladder cancer in humans. They had not. The historical question concerns what the industry knew about preliminary results and what happened to research it financed. The interpretation of the funding decision belongs to the document analysis, not to an imagined conversation in an office.

Dental research offered a further example. A 2015 historical study examined industry influence on the American National Caries Program. It found that substantial parts of an industry report entered the programme's first request for research proposals. Attention went toward ways of limiting dental damage while allowing sugar consumption to continue, whereas some research directly relevant to particular foods was left out.

The issue was the research agenda itself. If a programme concentrates on treating the consequences of consumption, it may leave less room for asking how to reduce exposure. That is a different mechanism from falsifying data, but it can still affect the knowledge available to policymakers.

It would nevertheless be inaccurate to say that American dietary advice simply ignored sugar for decades. The federal guidelines published in 1980 already advised people to avoid too much of it. They also discussed fat and other aspects of diet. The historical record is more complicated than a successful industry campaign making every official recommendation say the same thing.

How to read a conflict of interest

Industry funding did not end with those historical cases. Modern research papers often disclose sponsors and other financial relationships. That disclosure is useful, but it does not settle how a study should be judged. The methods, data and interpretation still need examination.

A review published in 2013 compared systematic reviews of sweetened drinks and weight gain. It found a difference between conclusions associated with declared industry conflicts and those without reported conflicts. Reviews in the first group more often judged the evidence insufficient to establish an association. The sample was small, so the much repeated percentages need their denominators to be meaningful.

The finding gives a reason to examine financial relationships carefully. It does not allow a reader to dismiss every industry funded paper or accept every other paper without scrutiny. An undisclosed relationship is a problem, but a disclosed relationship is not proof that a result is false.

Influence can also occur before a paper exists. A sponsor can choose to support one question rather than another. A research programme about physical activity may produce useful work while leaving the role of a company's drinks outside its scope. Asking who chose the question is therefore as important as asking whether the final calculations were done correctly.

The documentary behind this story describes companies supporting health projects and university posts. The institutions it contacted denied interference in research and teaching. Those responses belong in the account. Sponsorship can create a potential conflict without proving that a particular scientist was instructed to produce a particular result.

The same care is needed with public information. A website offering advice on teeth or nutrition may look independent while being funded by an interested organization. Clear disclosure helps readers understand who is speaking. It does not replace an assessment of the advice, but it gives readers information they should not have to discover through an investigation.

The fight for children's attention

Advertising works at a different point in the chain. It does not have to win an argument about blood sugar. It has to make a product familiar, desirable or easy to remember. A cartoon character, a sports star or a favourite online personality can help achieve that.

Children encounter food marketing through more than television. It can appear in entertainment, on social platforms and alongside activities they enjoy. The boundaries between an advertisement and the surrounding content may not always be obvious to the person watching.

In its 2023 guidance, the World Health Organization described evidence that food marketing affects children's preferences, intake and requests to adults. That does not mean every advertisement controls every child. It means that the pattern of exposure is relevant to health and cannot be reduced to whether one parent said yes to one request.

Parents still make decisions. But they do so while companies spend money trying to shape the decisions children ask them to make. A discussion of parental responsibility is incomplete if it treats that commercial influence as part of the natural background rather than a deliberate activity.

Restrictions on marketing are therefore different from banning a family from buying a product. They concern how a product is promoted and to whom. There can be real disagreements over definitions, enforcement and where the line should be drawn. Those disagreements are more useful when the actual measure is described accurately.

Inside the policy debate

In Germany, the interests involved extend beyond sugar producers. Farmers, food manufacturers, drink companies, retailers and advertising businesses may all have something at stake. Their interests are not identical, but several can oppose a measure that would make a familiar product harder to promote or more expensive to sell.

Lobbying is not automatically corruption. Governments need information from people affected by proposed rules, including businesses and workers. The problem is whether access is balanced, relationships are transparent and public health evidence receives an adequate hearing. A meeting with a minister proves access, not necessarily an unlawful agreement.

The documentary interviews Renate Künast, who was responsible for food and agriculture policy in the German government from 2001 to 2005. She recalls strong resistance when she tried to address unhealthy diets and advertising. Her account describes pressure reaching beyond her own ministry. These are her recollections, rather than an independently verified record of every conversation.

The documentary also describes later attempts under Christian Schmidt and Julia Klöckner to negotiate change with industry. In the account concerning Schmidt, he acknowledged that cooperation had been difficult, while qualifying how he understood discussions with party colleagues. That qualification matters. Reporting political pressure should not silently convert every participant's account into agreement about what happened.

Round tables can bring useful knowledge together. They can also leave a government dependent on the willingness of companies to accept changes that affect their sales. The outcome depends on who participates, what commitments are made and what happens if those commitments are missed.

There is a practical difference between a promise and a requirement. A voluntary target may encourage progress, especially when businesses see advantages in changing their products. A binding rule adds consequences for failing to comply. Neither approach should be judged solely by the ambition of its announcement. The relevant question is what changes afterwards.

Reading the packet and measuring progress

Food labels are one way of giving consumers more information. Under European rules, nutrition declarations became mandatory for most prepacked processed foods from December 2016. That was not the beginning of every kind of compulsory food labelling. Other requirements already existed, and the nutrition obligation has exceptions.

The sugar figure on a standard nutrition table describes total sugars. It does not separately tell the shopper how much is free sugar under the WHO definition. The ingredient list can provide additional clues about what has been added, but a shopper should not have to pretend that these two kinds of information answer exactly the same question.

Portion size adds another complication. Imagine two bottles with the same sugar concentration, one twice the size of the other. Drinking the entire larger bottle provides twice as much sugar. Comparing the amount per hundred millilitres helps someone compare recipes, while looking at the amount in the bottle helps them understand what they actually drink. Both calculations are useful, but they answer different questions. A small serving printed on a label may not resemble the serving someone pours at home.

Labels also ask something of the person using them. Comparing products takes time and understanding. Someone shopping with a tired child or a limited budget may not examine every packet. Information is valuable, but its presence does not remove differences in price, availability or marketing.

Even a carefully informed shopper must choose from the food that is available and affordable in that particular shop.

Germany's voluntary reduction strategy provides a more direct example of why measurement matters. A study published in 2023 examined soft drink sales and sugar content from 2015 to 2021. It found that the average sugar concentration, weighted by sales, had fallen by about two percent in Germany. The industry's target was a fifteen percent reduction by 2025, using 2015 as the baseline.

That study was an interim assessment. It could show that the observed pace was slow, but it could not report a final result for a year that had not yet arrived. The distinction prevents an early warning from turning into a falsely dated conclusion.

Using comparable data, the same study found a decline of about twenty nine percent in the United Kingdom over the same period. This was a measure of sugar concentration in soft drinks sold, not a percentage fall in every person's total dietary sugar. It also did not mean that the number of people with diabetes had fallen by that amount.

The phrase weighted by sales matters here. An ordinary average would give a rarely purchased drink the same importance as a popular one. Weighting the figures by sales gives more influence to the products people buy most. The result can change because manufacturers alter recipes or because shoppers buy a different mix of drinks. Looking at the average alone cannot tell us how much each of those changes contributed. Researchers need further information to separate them.

Changing the incentives

The United Kingdom announced its Soft Drinks Industry Levy in 2016 and introduced it in 2018. Its structure gave producers an incentive to reduce sugar concentration, since drinks above specified thresholds faced a levy. A company could respond by changing a recipe rather than only increasing the price.

That mechanism matters because it reaches people who never read a public health campaign. If a commonly purchased drink contains less sugar, consumers may receive less from that product without making a new decision at every purchase. Whether total intake falls also depends on how purchases change and what people choose instead.

A levy is not a complete nutrition policy. Its design affects which products are covered, what substitutes become attractive and how costs are shared. Evaluations need to consider these responses rather than assume that the policy has the same effect on every household.

Suppose a manufacturer reduces the sugar in a drink, but customers begin buying larger bottles. Some of the reduction per glass could be offset by the amount consumed. Alternatively, people might switch to water, adding to the effect of the recipe change. These are illustrations, not claims about what happened in every country. They explain why a useful evaluation follows several measures at once: recipes, sales volumes, household purchases and, where possible, changes in diet. A favourable number deserves attention, followed by a careful look at what it measures.

Chile offers an example of several measures introduced together. Its food policy combined warning labels, marketing restrictions and rules affecting sales in schools. A study of household beverage purchases found a decline in purchases of products classified as high in relevant nutrients compared with the pattern expected from earlier trends.

Purchases of other drinks increased, so the result should not be described as an equally large fall in all drinks or all sugar. Nor could the study isolate the effect of each part of the policy package. The useful lesson is that the food environment can change through several connected measures, and the consequences can be studied rather than merely asserted.

Campaigners also propose better food standards in schools, more opportunities for physical activity and making healthier foods more affordable. These address different problems. Exercise has benefits of its own, but it is not a reason to ignore diet. A healthier school meal does not remove advertising outside school. Combining measures requires attention to how they work together.

A different ending in Germany

The political situation changed after the period described in much of the documentary. On 14 October 2026, the German cabinet backed a proposal intended to introduce a tax on sugary drinks from July 2027. More precisely, it approved wording for an amendment that the governing parliamentary groups could bring into the legislative process.

This was a significant step beyond simply rejecting a levy. It was not proof that a final law had already taken effect. Parliamentary consideration, implementation and later evaluation remained distinct from the cabinet announcement. A story ending with an unqualified claim that the government still refused any such measure would therefore be out of date.

The change does not erase the earlier arguments over voluntary commitments or commercial influence. It changes the next questions. What will the final measure cover? Will companies alter their products? How will prices and purchasing respond? Will the results justify the claims made for it?

For a family at the breakfast table, those questions may feel distant. Yet the products on the table reflect choices made long before anyone opened the fridge. Recipes, prices, advertising and public rules all helped shape what was available. People make decisions within that setting, and changing the setting can make different decisions easier.

The case for prevention does not require treating every sweet food as poison or every person who enjoys one as irresponsible. It requires taking avoidable harm seriously and being honest about what the evidence can show. A policy should be open to criticism, just as an industry's assurances should be open to examination.

The next chapter will be written through those ordinary details: what manufacturers put into drinks, what children are encouraged to ask for, what schools serve and what households can afford. Personal choices remain part of the story. So do the decisions that determine which choices are easiest to make.

title: DMT and the feeling of reality
body:
A room that seems to disappear

The person lying in a research room has not physically travelled anywhere. Yet, after receiving DMT, the room may seem to disappear. Colours, spaces and apparent figures can replace familiar surroundings. Some people describe fear, others wonder. A few minutes can feel detached from ordinary time. When the effects fade, explaining what happened can be harder than describing a dream.

DMT is short for dimethyltryptamine. The substance discussed here is usually written more precisely as N,N dimethyltryptamine. It belongs to a group of drugs called psychedelics, which can profoundly alter perception and the sense of self. Calling it the strongest psychedelic in the world would suggest a simple ranking that does not exist. Intensity, duration and physical effects are different questions.

The documentary behind this story introduces a participant it calls Sarah. In its account, frightening patterns give way to playful figures and a feeling of encountering another presence. These are reports of her experience. They do not establish that an independent being entered the room or that she travelled to another universe. Still, the experience felt important to her, and that feeling itself deserves investigation.

This is what makes DMT interesting to researchers. The question is not only why someone sees unusual images. It is also how an experience can acquire such certainty. What makes an imagined place feel real? Why does a perceived figure seem to have intentions? And can studying those changes tell us something about ordinary consciousness?

A plant with a history

Long before laboratory researchers studied DMT, Indigenous communities in the Amazon had knowledge of psychoactive plants and preparations. These practices belonged to particular cultures, with their own meanings and traditions. They were not waiting for a European visitor to make them significant. A botanical description records one kind of knowledge, but it does not replace the knowledge of the people using a plant.

In the nineteenth century, the English botanist Richard Spruce encountered preparations known by names including caapi and ayahuasca during his travels in South America. He collected plant material and described what he observed. The experiences puzzled him. The tools needed to identify all the relevant chemicals were not available to him in the way they are to researchers today.

It is tempting to tell this as a story in which Spruce collected the wrong plant and missed the real ingredient. That would be misleading. The vine now called Banisteriopsis caapi has an important pharmacological role. It contains compounds that affect the breakdown of other substances in the body. It is not simply an inactive container for something found elsewhere.

Ayahuasca and isolated DMT should therefore not be treated as identical. A preparation commonly studied by scientists combines DMT with plant compounds that inhibit enzymes responsible for its breakdown. This interaction can allow DMT to have effects when swallowed. Preparations vary, and their other ingredients also matter. The chemistry helps explain the combination without telling us exactly what was in every historical cup.

The names of related substances require equal care. Another psychedelic often discussed alongside DMT is known as 5 MeO DMT. It is a different compound. An experience or treatment result involving one cannot automatically be assigned to the other. Similar names are not evidence that the substances have identical effects or risks.

Research returns to the laboratory

DMT acts on receptors involved in serotonin signalling, including the serotonin 2A receptor. Serotonin is a chemical messenger with many functions. The fact that a drug affects this system does not reduce its action to a simple change in happiness. Perception, emotion and the processing of information involve interacting systems, not one chemical switch for each feeling.

During the twentieth century, interest in psychedelics spread beyond laboratories into popular culture. The documentary describes Terence McKenna, whose accounts of strange spaces and apparently intelligent figures became influential. His interpretations went beyond describing what he felt. He proposed that these experiences revealed something hidden about reality. That is a philosophical claim, distinct from an observation a laboratory can independently confirm.

Legal restrictions also changed the conditions of research. The United Nations Convention on Psychotropic Substances was adopted in 1971 and entered into force in 1976. It established international controls while recognizing medical and scientific uses. Research became difficult under restrictive systems, but saying that every investigation stopped everywhere would erase the differences between countries, institutions and periods.

In the 1990s, psychiatrist Rick Strassman helped renew controlled human research with DMT in the United States. His published studies measured both bodily responses and participants' descriptions. They reported rapid changes in perception and emotion alongside effects such as increased blood pressure and heart rate. These were supervised experiments with selected volunteers, not demonstrations that the substance was harmless in any setting.

Strassman's popular description of DMT as a spirit molecule captured the character of some accounts. It was a memorable phrase, not a scientific classification showing that a molecule carries a spirit. The words helped frame a public conversation in which laboratory findings, personal meaning and spiritual interpretation often became difficult to separate.

Listening without assuming

Reports of encounters are among the most striking parts of that conversation. People may describe guides, unfamiliar beings or figures that seem to communicate without speech. Some experiences are comforting. Others are frightening or confusing. A researcher can take the report seriously without deciding that its explanation must be literally correct.

A survey published in 2020 gathered responses from 2,561 people about apparent entity encounters after DMT. Participants were asked to recall their most memorable encounter. The design matters: the researchers selected people who had something of this kind to report. The survey could describe those accounts, but it could not establish how often such experiences occur among everyone who uses DMT.

An online account also reaches a researcher through several filters. Someone has to remember the event, choose words for it and decide to share it. The person reading it then has to interpret those words. Two people might use the same label for rather different experiences, or different labels for experiences that overlap. Numbers do not remove those difficulties.
