On Tuesday, the same sound came at six forty five. On Wednesday, it came while she was already awake, waiting for it.

That annoyed her more than the noise itself.

She composed a message in her head while brushing her teeth. It began with "Some of us are trying to sleep" and became less polite from there.

By the time she left for work, she had decided not to put that message through anyone's door.

On the stairs

That evening, Iris met a man on the landing carrying a small plant and a bag of oranges. One orange rolled from the bag and stopped against her shoe.

She picked it up.

"I think this is yours."

"Thank you. The bag has decided it's finished."

He shifted the plant to his other arm. Iris held the torn bag while he found his keys.

"I'm Noah. I've just moved in upstairs."

"Iris. Directly below you."

He smiled.

"Then I'm sorry about Saturday. The mattress was more difficult than expected."

"I was out for most of it."

She almost left the conversation there. He seemed tired, and the plant was slowly sliding down his sleeve. But she did not want another morning of lying in bed, angry with someone who had no idea why.

"There is one thing, actually. I hear something dragging across the floor early in the morning. Around quarter to seven. It wakes me up."

Noah frowned, looking up toward his flat as if the answer might be visible through the ceiling.

"My kitchen chair, probably. I eat before leaving for work."

"It sounds quite loud downstairs."

"I didn't realise. Thank you for telling me."

A small experiment

Noah put the plant and oranges inside, then came back to the landing.

"Could we check? I can move the chair while you're in your flat. Then we'll know whether that's it."

Iris agreed. They exchanged numbers for the test, and she went downstairs. In her bedroom, she sent a message saying she was ready.

The familiar scrape crossed the ceiling.

"That's it", she wrote.

A moment later, a second sound came, softer and shorter.

"I lifted it that time", Noah replied.

She could still hear a small bump, but nothing like the first noise.

They met on the landing again.

"The kitchen must be right over your room", he said. "I'll get pads for the chair legs. Until then, I'll lift it."

"Thank you. I don't expect you to stop having breakfast."

"Good. I'm not pleasant without it."

She smiled. The speech she had prepared that morning would have sounded ridiculous now.

What the walls carried

On Friday, Noah sent a short message asking whether the chair was better.

Iris had forgotten to listen for it.

"Yes. Much better. Thank you."

She was about to put the phone away when another message arrived.

"Can I ask something too? Is there a television against the wall in your living room?"

There was. Iris looked at it.

"Yes. Can you hear it?"

"Mostly the low sounds. Last night I thought someone was moving furniture until I heard the music."

She had watched a film with a long scene involving a helicopter. The television had been playing through a small speaker on the floor.

"That's probably mine. I'll move the speaker and lower the bass. Let me know if it's still a problem."

After changing the settings, she played a short part of the same scene at her usual volume. Noah listened upstairs and messaged that it was much less noticeable.

Iris put the speaker on a suitable stand away from their shared wall. She also lowered the volume for the rest of the evening. She had been so busy noticing his chair that she had never wondered what he could hear from her flat.

The spare oranges

On Sunday afternoon, there was a knock at Iris's door. Noah held a small bowl of oranges.

"A replacement for the one you rescued. Plus some extras. I bought too many."

"You don't owe me an orange."

"Then consider it help with a storage problem."

She took the bowl and invited him in for coffee. This time, he was not carrying a plant, and neither of them needed to hurry out to work.

Noah asked where she bought bread. Iris told him about the bakery near the bus stop, including the fact that it closed early on Sundays. He told her that the small hardware shop had the chair pads behind the counter, not on the shelves where he had spent ten minutes looking.

When he left, Iris washed the bowl and dried it. She put two slices of the cake she had made inside, then carried it upstairs.

Noah opened the door.

"The bowl is becoming a delivery service", he said.

"Only until one of us stops returning it."

From behind him came the sound of a chair being lifted and set down carefully. His visiting sister appeared in the kitchen doorway.

"Like that?" she asked.

Noah looked at Iris.

"She's learning the local customs."

title: The missing cat
body:
An empty chair

Milo was not on the kitchen chair. He was not behind the curtain, under the bed or in the laundry basket, where he sometimes slept on clean towels.

Sara checked the basket twice.

"Milo?"

Her cat usually appeared as soon as she opened the cupboard containing his food. This time, the sound brought nobody.

She had been carrying bags in from the car that morning. The front door had stood open for a few minutes while her cousin Ben helped with a heavy box. Milo might have slipped out then.

Or he might still be asleep somewhere she had not looked.

Sara searched the flat carefully, including the cupboard she had opened while putting things away. Ben checked behind the sofa, then straightened up with a dusty tennis ball.

"Not a cat."

"I can see that."

He put the ball on the table.

"Let's work out where we haven't looked."

A clear description

They checked the stairwell and the shared entrance. Sara called Milo softly, then stopped to listen. A washing machine hummed behind a closed door. Nothing moved on the stairs.

In the courtyard, their neighbour Dina was taking dry sheets from a line.

"Have you seen my cat this morning?" Sara asked.

"Remind me what he looks like."

"Grey, with white paws. His front left paw has a little grey patch on it."

"Big or small?"

"Quite small. No collar."

Sara opened a recent photograph on her phone. Milo lay across a newspaper, making most of the headline unreadable.

Dina studied it.

"I saw a grey cat by the bins, but that was yesterday. I can't say it was him."

"Thank you. Could you let me know if you see him again?"

"Of course. Have you checked the storage rooms?"

Sara looked toward the row of doors at the back of the courtyard. One had been open earlier, when someone was moving garden chairs.

The locked door

They did not know who used the first room. Dina knew that Mr Cole kept his gardening tools in the second, so she knocked at his flat and asked whether he could check it with them.

He came down carrying a ring of keys.

"I had the door open this morning", he said. "Only for a few minutes."

"That's all he'd need", Sara replied.

Mr Cole opened the room. They waited outside the doorway while Sara called. There were folded chairs, empty plant pots and a bag of compost. No cat appeared.

With Mr Cole's permission, they looked behind the larger things without moving the heavy stack of chairs. Sara crouched beside a pot and found a glove.

"One of mine", Mr Cole said. "Missing since March."

Sara tried to smile.

They left the room as they had found it. Mr Cole said he would keep an eye out and ask his wife about the other storage door.

Ben suggested they return to the flat for a moment. Sara was calling faster now, hardly leaving a gap between Milo's name and the next call.

"We can make a short notice with that photo", he said. "And check the flat once more."

The notice on the screen

At the kitchen table, Sara chose a photograph that showed all four paws. She wrote a description, the area where Milo had last been seen and a contact number.

Ben read it before she posted it in the building's residents group.

"You wrote that he escaped into the courtyard. We don't know that."

She changed it to say that he might have left through the front door that morning.

"Better?"

"Yes."

She asked neighbours to check enclosed spaces they had opened that day and to contact her if they saw him. Then she called her usual veterinary practice to tell them he was missing and check what information they needed. She noted their advice and checked that her contact details on Milo's microchip registration were current.

Her phone buzzed before she had put down the pen.

A message from Mr Cole.

"My wife says the first room belongs to the upstairs flat. They're home now."

A very small sound

The neighbour upstairs was called June. She had been putting away camping equipment that morning and came down with her key as soon as Sara explained.

At the first storage door, Sara heard a faint scrape from inside.

Everyone stopped talking.

Then came a short, annoyed sound that she knew very well.

June opened the door carefully. Milo was sitting on a folded blanket behind a camping bag, looking as if the delay had been someone else's fault.

Sara crouched and spoke to him. Ben brought the carrier from her flat while June kept the doorway clear. Once Milo had come close enough, Sara settled him into it and closed the door securely.

She stayed crouching for another moment, one hand on top of the carrier.

"There you are."

Dina, watching from the courtyard, took a sheet off her arm.

"Grey cat. White paws. Very unimpressed."

The update

Back upstairs, Milo drank some water and returned to the kitchen chair. Sara watched him settle, then sent an update to the residents group saying he had been found. She thanked everyone who had helped and let the veterinary practice know too.

Ben picked up the tennis ball from the table.

"We found this as well. A productive morning."

"Don't call it that yet."

Sara put a note beside the front door to remind herself to keep Milo in a closed room when carrying things in. Then she checked the latch and finally sat down.

Milo opened one eye from the chair opposite.

Ben lowered his voice.

"Should we tell him everyone was worried?"

"I think he's waiting for an apology."

title: The first order
body:
A promising message

At nine on Monday morning, Lina received the message she had been waiting for.

"We would like you to make our new price cards. Could you have them ready by Friday?"

The message came from a small flower shop near the station. Lina had recently started designing printed materials for local businesses. Until then, most of her work had been birthday invitations for relatives, who paid her with dinner and asked for changes over dessert.

This would be her first proper order.

She typed, "Of course!" Then she stopped with her finger above the send button.

How many cards? What size? Did Friday mean Friday morning or the end of the day?

She deleted the answer and asked whether she could visit the shop that afternoon.

Paper and flowers

The owner, Ruth, was carrying a bucket when Lina arrived. She pointed toward a counter covered in ribbon, scissors and small pieces of paper.

"Those are the old cards. We need something clearer."

Lina picked one up. The price was written in pale green, with a flower above it. From the other side of the counter, she could barely read the number.

"Will you use them inside or in the window?"

"Both. And outside when the weather is good."

Lina wrote that down.

They counted twelve kinds of plant that needed permanent cards. Ruth also wanted blank cards for changing offers. She expected the price to include printing. Lina had been thinking only about the design.

For a moment, she wished she had already said yes. It would have felt easier than explaining what she did not yet know.

Instead, she closed her notebook halfway.

"I can price the design today. I need to ask the printer about suitable paper and delivery before I can give you a total."

Ruth nodded.

"Please do. I don't want to discover on Thursday that printing costs extra."

They agreed that ready meant delivered to the shop before ten on Friday morning. Ruth would send the final names and prices that evening. Lina would prepare one sample before laying out the whole set.

The sample

The printer recommended a firm card for indoor use and explained that ordinary paper would not last outside in rain. Ruth already owned clear holders, so Lina measured those before leaving.

That evening, she sent a written quote. It listed the design, one round of changes, the number of printed cards and the delivery time. Extra copies would cost more. Ruth accepted it the next morning.

Lina opened her drawing program and spent an hour making a border of tiny leaves.

She liked the leaves. She tried them in three colours.

Then she printed the sample at its actual size and placed it across the kitchen table.

The leaves looked lovely. The price looked small.

She made the price larger and removed half the border. When she sent the sample to Ruth, she included a photograph of it in a holder, beside a ruler.

The reply arrived during lunch.

"Much easier to read. Can the shop name be a little smaller? And that plant costs eight euros, not six."

Lina checked the list. It said six.

She began a reply explaining this, then decided a phone call would be quicker.

"I can change it," she told Ruth. "Could you check all twelve prices now, so I use one final list?"

There was a pause, followed by the sound of a drawer closing.

"Yes. Two others changed last week. I'll send a new list and mark it final."

A late addition

By Wednesday afternoon, Ruth had approved the complete set. Lina was about to send the file to the printer when another message appeared.

"Could we add a large poster for the window? Same style. It should be quick."

Lina looked at the time. She wanted Ruth to recommend her to other shops. She also knew that making a poster meant checking another size, arranging more text and getting another printing price.

She called the printer first.

Then she answered Ruth.

"The cards can still be ready on Friday. I can also design the poster, but I need the wording and approval separately. I can send you a price for Monday delivery."

Ruth chose to wait until the following week. She had not realised the printer needed a separate file.

Lina sent the cards to print and ate the lunch she had left beside her keyboard. It was nearly four. The cheese had gone warm.

Friday morning

At half past nine on Friday, Lina carried a flat box into the flower shop. Ruth cleared a space on the counter. Together, they checked the quantities and compared the printed prices with the approved list.

One holder was narrower than the others. Its card would not slide in.

Lina felt her face grow hot. Then Ruth turned the holder around and pulled out an old piece of cardboard stuck inside.

"Found the problem."

The new card fitted.

Ruth put three cards in the window and stepped outside to look. Lina followed her.

"Yes," Ruth said. "I can read those without my glasses. Send me the invoice."

On her way home, Lina bought a sandwich. She sat on a bench and opened her notebook to a clean page.

At the top, she wrote, "Next order."

Underneath, she added three questions about size, quantity and deadline. Then, remembering the warm cheese, she put a lunch break into her calendar.

title: The wrong file
body:
Before the meeting

At twenty past eight, Tom had one hand on his coat and the other on his mouse. He worked in the office of a community centre, and the coordinator was waiting for the programme of Saturday's activities.

The meeting started at nine. His bus left in six minutes.

He attached the file, wrote a short message and pressed send.

Then he picked up his bag, put down his bag, and went back for his lunch.

On the bus, he remembered something less useful than lunch. There were two copies of the programme on his computer. One was in the shared folder. The other was on his desktop, where he had saved it the previous afternoon before the pottery teacher called.

The pottery class had moved from eleven to twelve. The room had changed too.

Tom opened his sent message on his phone. The attachment was called Saturday Programme.

That did not help. Both copies had the same name.

He opened the attachment itself. Beside pottery, it said eleven, room two.

The first call

Tom looked at the clock. It was eight thirty four. He could wait until he reached the office and explain in person. Perhaps nobody had opened the message yet.

Then he imagined twelve copies of the wrong programme on the meeting table.

He called the coordinator, Eva.

"I've sent you yesterday's version," he said. "The pottery time and room are wrong. Please don't print that attachment."

"I already printed one copy. Is it only the pottery class?"

"That's the change I remember. I need to compare the files before I say it's the only one. I'll be there in about ten minutes."

"All right. I'll mark this copy as old. Check the rest when you arrive."

Tom put his phone away. He had expected a longer conversation, perhaps a disappointed silence. Instead, Eva had asked a practical question, and he had not yet given her a complete answer.

At the next stop, a passenger squeezed past him with a folded pushchair. Tom moved his bag and nearly left his lunch on the seat.

Two versions

In the office, he took off his coat and opened both files side by side.

The pottery class was not the only difference. The walking group now met at the side entrance because the main hall would be used for a sale. He had forgotten that change altogether.

He checked the revised programme against the messages from the activity leaders. Then he asked his colleague Nia to read the times and room numbers aloud while he followed the list.

"You're very quiet this morning," she said.

"I'm trying not to make a second mistake while fixing the first."

Nia pulled her chair closer.

They found no further differences. Tom exported a fresh copy with the revision date in its name, opened that exported file and checked it once more.

At eight fifty two, he sent it to Eva. His message named the two corrections and asked her to use this attachment instead of the earlier one.

Then he walked to the meeting room with a printed copy.

Eva was arranging chairs.

"This is the replacement?"

"Yes. Pottery at twelve in room four. The walking group meets at the side entrance. Everything else matches the confirmed list."

She crossed out the front page of the old copy and put it in the paper recycling box.

One more place

After the meeting, Tom felt ready for coffee. Nia stopped him at the kitchen door.

"Did the desk get the first version too?"

He stood still.

He had sent it to reception late the previous day, when the afternoon changes were still arriving. They kept a copy for people who asked about weekend activities.

"I'll check."

At reception, a yellow sheet lay beside the phone. Tom recognised his old programme. He explained the corrections to Jo, who worked there that morning, and replaced the sheet.

"Has anyone asked about pottery?" he said.

Jo looked at the notes beside her keyboard.

"One caller. I told her eleven. She asked me to reserve a place, so I have her number in the booking system. I'll call and explain the change."

Tom waited while she made the call. The new time suited the caller. Jo updated the booking note and turned back to him.

"Anything else changing?"

"Nothing confirmed. If something does, I'll send you a replacement and say exactly what's different."

A smaller folder

That afternoon, Tom and Nia looked at the shared folder. It contained six files with Saturday in the name. Two included the word final.

Neither was the version they had used that morning.

They agreed to keep the current programme in one clearly labelled folder and move older versions into an archive. They would use dates in exported filenames and check the attachment before sending it. Eva agreed to the arrangement.

Tom moved his desktop copy into the archive as well. For a moment, the empty space on the screen looked oddly noticeable.

At five, he sent Nia the confirmed programme for the following staff shift. He opened the attachment from the draft message before pressing send.

"Twelve o'clock," he said quietly. "Room four. Side entrance."

Nia looked up.

"Talking to the computer?"

"Checking what it plans to tell people."

He shut it down, picked up his bag and reached for his coat.

Then he remembered his lunch. It was still in the office fridge, exactly where he had put it that morning.

title: A difficult handover
body:
Ten minutes together

When Priya arrived at the bicycle shop, Dan was talking on the phone, a customer was waiting at the counter and a small dog was licking the leg of a display stand.

Their shifts overlapped by ten minutes. Usually, that was enough.

Dan covered the phone with his hand.

"Blue bike's ready. Red one needs a call. Delivery at three. Everything's in the book."

Priya put her bag under the counter.

"Which blue bike?"

There were two near the collection area. One had a basket. The other had a child seat.

Dan pointed, but the customer stepped between them at the same moment. Priya saw a finger and the back of a coat.

Then Dan returned to his call.

The waiting customer wanted a new bell. Priya showed him three, let him try them and explained how they fitted. His dog stopped licking the stand and looked offended by each sound.

By the time the customer left, seven of their ten minutes had gone.

The open book

Dan picked up his jacket.

"Sorry. I need to catch the bus. Can you call if anything's unclear?"

Priya looked at the open notebook. Under red bike, someone had written, "Ask about wheel."

"One minute before you go. I can't tell what this means."

Dan put the jacket down again.

"The customer needs to approve a replacement wheel."

"Have we given her a price?"

"I think so. Ask Mark."

Mark, the mechanic, was behind the workshop door. Priya could hear a pump and a radio.

She turned back a page. There were several crossed out entries and a phone number with no name beside it. She did not know whether it belonged to the owner of the red bicycle.

"Let's use the job numbers," she said. "Otherwise I might call the wrong person."

Dan opened the repair system on the shop computer.

They found the red bicycle under job forty two. The customer's number was there, along with Mark's estimate. No approval had been recorded.

"So I call her with the estimate, and Mark waits for her answer?"

"Yes. That's it."

Priya wrote the next action beside the job number, then added her own name.

Which one is ready?

The blue bicycle with the basket was job thirty eight. Its repair was finished and the safety check was recorded. The customer had been told she could collect it after two.

The blue bicycle with the child seat was still waiting for a part.

Dan looked at the two bikes.

"I should have said basket."

"The number is better. We might have three baskets tomorrow."

He smiled, but Priya could see him glance at the clock.

"I'll finish the notes," she said. "Tell me about the delivery."

It was a box of inner tubes, expected around three, not a bicycle delivery. The order reference was in the system. Priya needed to check the quantity against the delivery note before signing and put the box on the stock shelf.

She repeated the three tasks aloud. Dan corrected one detail: the tubes belonged on the lower shelf, not the upper one, which held returned items.

Then he left at his scheduled time. Priya still had a page of untidy notes, but she knew what each line meant.

A question for the workshop

Before calling the owner of the red bicycle, Priya went to find Mark.

"The estimate says the wheel and fitting are included. Is there anything else I need to explain?"

Mark stopped pumping a tyre.

"The wheel has to be ordered. If she agrees today, I'll confirm a collection date once the supplier confirms delivery. Don't promise tomorrow."

Priya added that to her notes.

The customer answered on the fourth ring. Priya gave the price and explained the timing. The customer asked whether she could think about it until the next morning.

"Of course. I'll record that we're waiting for your decision. No replacement wheel will be ordered yet."

After the call, Priya updated the repair record and told Mark. She crossed the completed call off her own list, leaving the customer's decision clearly marked as pending.

At quarter past two, the owner of the blue bicycle arrived. Priya checked the job number and brought out the bicycle with the basket.

The basket contained one glove.

"I've been looking for that all week," the customer said.

Priya decided not to mention that the bicycle had only been in the shop since yesterday.

The next afternoon

The delivery arrived twenty minutes late. Priya checked it, put it on the correct shelf and recorded that it had arrived. At closing time, she could see which tasks were finished without trying to remember every conversation.

When Dan came in the next day, he brought two coffees.

"One is an apology for the blue bike instructions."

"Which one?"

He looked down at the identical cups, then laughed.

"The one without sugar. Wait, let me check."

Over coffee, they agreed on a short handover routine: job number, current situation, next action and who would do it. Anything unfinished would stay visible in the repair system.

They also asked the manager for five protected minutes together before each shift ended. One person would cover the counter while the other two handed over.

That afternoon, Dan's first note began with a job number. Priya read it and asked one question. He answered it, put on his jacket and caught his bus.
